speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This framework has worked well for us thus far.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Most employers have fair employment practices and our surveys show a declining trend of workplace discrimination over the years.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: However, we are also contending with an ageing population and economic headwinds.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Amidst these demographic and economic realities, a complementary foreign workforce remains important to Singapore's continued economic success as well as ensuring good jobs and good wages for locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But we are also clear that these benefits will only accrue to Singaporeans if there is a level playing field that prevents discriminatory practices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This allows all employees to grasp the opportunities in our vibrant economy.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, even as we have made progress, we must not take our generally harmonious and fair workplace conditions for granted.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is the result of close cooperation amongst tripartite partners – the Government, the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) – to develop a balanced approach.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have taken in the Labour Movement's feedback, such as through the Professionals, Managers and Executives, or PME, Taskforce and Every Worker Matters Conversations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we have taken note of SNEF's views on the need to provide operational flexibility for employers, so they can apply fair employment practices while meeting genuine business needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have also studied other countries with anti-discrimination laws.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, different countries have different national contexts and so, the laws are not quite comparable across countries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, the characteristics that are legally protected and how disputes are legally resolved, differ from country to country.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, introducing such laws is complex, and well-meaning legal protections for workers can have unintended consequences that end up hurting workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, if employers become more reluctant to hire certain groups or the laws result in protracted litigation between employers and employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have taken the time to consult and study these experiences carefully, instead of rushing to introduce and implement the Bill, because we want to keep our hard-earned harmony in our workplaces and society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The comprehensive process that we have gone through and the effort we have made to understand different stakeholder groups give us confidence that the Bill strikes the right balance for now.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the end of the day, employers must fundamentally be able to hire employees based on the skills and attributes that support their business needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What we want to achieve is to ensure that jobseekers and employees are evaluated fairly based on those skills and those attributes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even as we take this next step in our workplace fairness journey, please also let me emphasise upfront that Workplace Fairness Legislation (WFL) is not a panacea.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Rather, it is an additional layer of protection that allows us to take certain actions against the more frequently encountered forms of workplace discrimination where there is societal consensus today.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is a measured approach that seeks to preserve our current workplace norms and guard against divisions in our workplaces and society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I will now cover how the Bill will: first, strengthen protections for jobseekers and employees against discrimination, while retaining flexibility for employers; second, provide grievance handling processes to promote better communication and amicable resolution of issues; and third, complement our education-first approach, with calibrated levers, to deal with the small number of bad employers who persist in egregious discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Singapore is a meritocracy and employers here must hire and assess workers based on their ability to do the job well.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Every worker should also have the opportunity to develop their potential, without employment decisions being distorted by discriminatory biases.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, let me explain how the Bill gives effect to this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Bill prohibits employers from making an adverse employment decision on the ground of a protected characteristic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Under clause 17 read with clauses 5, 6, and 7, employers are prohibited from choosing not to hire someone, or giving them a poor performance appraisal, denying a promotion or training opportunity or dismissing them because the jobseeker or employee has a protected characteristic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Bill will also prohibit company policies or job advertisements that discriminate on the ground of a protected characteristic under clauses 18 and 19.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: These are areas where there is broad societal consensus and we have national policy imperatives to prevent discrimination against in the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This provides some assurance that we have the requisite experience and the capabilities to handle such cases under WFL, without disrupting business operations or workplace harmony.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Bill protects age discrimination because all workers, young and old, deserve to be assessed based on how well they do their jobs rather than their age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, employers should not assume that an older worker or an older person has less strength than a young person to carry out manual tasks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we also recognise that senior workers are disproportionately impacted by age discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Given our ageing population, we must empower our senior workers to contribute to our workforce if they wish to, for as long as they remain productive and continue learning and refreshing their skills.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, this is why an exception under clause 21 provides employers with the flexibility if they intend to tap on these seniors' experience and expertise and retain them in the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we also know that the law can only go so far in preventing discriminatory practices and we will continue our efforts to dispel negative stereotypes and create more age-inclusive workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Many Singaporeans understand the economic case for why we need foreigners.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They grow the economic pie by anchoring companies and investments that create better prospects for Singaporean workers and businesses.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They have been competing hard to attract more global talent so that they can anchor global and regional functions, cutting-edge technology and skills in emerging industries.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Without foreigners to complement our local workforce, we will lose out on better jobs, higher wages and stronger business opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, it is essential that we remain open, connected and welcoming to global talent and to businesses that can make our team stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we recognise the lived experiences and concerns of Singaporeans about whether foreigners are taking over their jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: From time to time, we hear of biased employment preferences for specific nationalities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have been taking strong measures to counter such discriminatory practices to ensure that our locals are treated fairly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Bill is our next step to further strengthen protections for Singaporeans and ensure a fair playing field.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will enable us to take stronger action against nationality discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have also gone a step further in clause 22, to provide an exception that will allow employers to make employment decisions based on whether the person is part of the local workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This means employers will be given the flexibility to strengthen their local workforce core, to build stronger local networks and greater resilience to disruptions like the recent pandemic and, hence, achieve stronger business outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The third category is sex, marital status, pregnancy and caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Based on earlier feedback, including from the Conversations on Singapore Women's Development, these areas are important to ensure fair, merit-based treatment for men and women alike and to support our national marriage and parenthood objectives.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, this is why the Bill protects against discrimination on the basis of sex, which under clause 10 refers to the sex that is legally assigned to the individual, either at birth or post re-assignment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While we have made progress, women continue to be underrepresented in areas, such as science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM) fields and leadership roles.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Women's participation on the boards of the top 100 Singapore Exchange-listed companies is currently 25%.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We recognise that this could be due to an interplay of many social and economic factors.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Government will keep working hard to empower women to fulfil their aspirations and we hope this Bill can contribute towards our efforts for a more balanced representation of men and women across sectors and across occupations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The protection for caregivers is in line with the Government's efforts to build a family-friendly environment in support of both fathers and mothers, in their marriage and parenthood journey, especially to signal the important role fathers play as an equal partner in the care of their children.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will also support the greater care needs for our ageing population.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The fourth category is race, religion and language ability.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While racial and religious harmony is part of our long-standing societal values, we still hear that some members of the minority races face racial discrimination at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, employers cannot assume that a person of another race does not know Malay or Mandarin.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This will send a strong statement that racial and religious discrimination are not acceptable in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Relatedly, clause 23 affords religious groups with some flexibility to make employment decisions for roles that are religious in nature, such as imams and priests, and roles related to the running of religious institutions, while preserving common space for secular jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is appropriate in view of Singapore's multi-religious society and the longstanding role that religious groups play in our social fabric.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The fifth category is disability and mental health conditions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have also received feedback on the importance of employers making accommodations for persons with disabilities to participate in the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To this end, we are working on a Tripartite Advisory for Reasonable Accommodations to raise awareness and to provide practical guidance to employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We hope this will help to bring the concept of reasonable accommodations into the mainstream employment space.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This greater public awareness will lay the foundation for future moves as part of our Enabling Masterplan, to further support persons with disabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For persons with mental health conditions, this Bill recognises that they are more likely to face challenges at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As raised multiple times in Parliament, mental health issues are a growing challenge, both in Singapore and globally.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We must take an evidence-based approach to mental health issues at the workplace, rather than perpetuate stigmas that limit the potential contributions of these fellow members of our society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Like us, other jurisdictions, such as Australia and Hong Kong, also have a positive list of protected characteristics as it is not practicable to legislate broad principles without causing uncertainty.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Just as each jurisdiction has its own bespoke set of protected characteristics, we decided on each protected characteristic for their own policy reasons which I have shared earlier, such as supporting our older workers to contribute to our ageing workforce amidst demographic constraints and reaffirming racial and religious harmony as part of our key societal values.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is also important to note that discrimination can arise in many ways.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It is a complex and nuanced topic which engages various socio-economic issues.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, indirect discrimination is when an employer takes an apparently neutral action that disadvantages people with a protected characteristic in practice.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It can impose very wide legal obligations that can create uncertainty and litigiousness for both employers and employees and we have seen cases overseas where employers who had standardised ability tests were challenged because certain racial groups tended to fare worse than others.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, examples like this remind us why it is important that our laws are not overly prescriptive.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is to avoid undermining labour market flexibility and inhibiting our ability to leverage our long-standing and successful model of labour relations to manage such complex issues.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, we have designed this Bill knowing it cannot be the only tool to tackle all forms of workplace discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Instead, this Bill starts on a more scoped and surer footing to ensure that we can preserve the precious workplace and social harmony that we enjoy today, while remaining open to future updates to the list of protected characteristics.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Internationally, this approach of having a law to cover certain protected characteristics with a more flexible tool to cover all other characteristics is quite unique.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It enables any employee who faces discrimination to seek support and is only made possible because of good tripartite relations and strong institutions, like TAFEP.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also update TGFEP in tandem with the WFL's implementation to ensure alignment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: You will not be turned away simply because it is not a protected characteristic.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: TGFEP will continue to cover all forms of workplace discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Next, I will talk about how the Bill provides room for genuine business needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Clause 20 sets out the ways that employers can legitimately consider protected characteristics when making employment decisions.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: First, for the reasonable performance of the job.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, an employer can consider if a jobseeker is fluent in a particular language for the role of an interpreter.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Second, for health and safety reasons, to protect employees and the people around them.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, a security company can consider whether an officer with a recently diagnosed but untreated case of depression can carry firearms, for the safety of the officer and for others.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, a spa can choose to hire female therapists to serve their female clientele.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For example, a bus company may only hire bus driver trainees above 21 years old because this is the regulatory age needed to obtain a bus driver's vocational licence.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In designing these flexibilities, we also want to assure employers that they will not run afoul of the law if they need to make employment decisions based on requirements set by the Government, such as those involving public safety or national security.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: TAFEP has seen disputes arise from miscommunication that could have been easily or quickly resolved if the parties had discussed openly from the start.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Workplace disputes should, where possible, be resolved within the firm itself.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This encourages employers and employees to settle differences more amicably whilst minimising disruptions and it also builds trust.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: By making a push for firms to put in place processes to handle grievances professionally and sensitively, we can help these employers ensure that genuine cases do not fall through the cracks.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Grievance handling processes will also help to build trust by providing a safe space to have conversations about sensitive or difficult issues.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Throughout the process, the employer must also protect the employee's confidentiality to the extent possible.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Bill focuses on ensuring that employers have a grievance handling process in place and it refrains from being overly prescriptive on the detailed requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This approach is a pragmatic, practical and a sensible one, given the diversity of firms in our economy – a process that works for a technology startup with 30 employees might not work for a construction company with 300 employees or a bank with 3,000 employees.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The grievance handling requirement will serve as a baseline requirement that most of our employees can benefit from.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Unions will continue to play a key role in setting the right norms, educating workers about their rights and amicably resolving disputes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For firms that do not already have such processes in place, TAFEP has prepared accessible and practical resources and templates.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For instance, there is a Grievance Handling Handbook on TAFEP's website that provides details on internal grievance handling procedures.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: TAFEP is also working on a new e-learning courseware to guide employers on how to implement the grievance handling process.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we know formal processes alone may not be sufficient.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In MOM's 2023 survey, we saw a decline in the proportion of employees who sought help after experiencing discrimination, despite a rise in firms with formal procedures.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employees were worried about impacting their work relationships or careers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The message we want to send out is clear: we will not hesitate to take action against employers that retaliate against those who raise valid grievances and employees should therefore feel safe to bring them up.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond these formal legal protections, MOM and TAFEP will continue our longer-term educational efforts so that employers and employees see the value of keeping communications and attitudes open.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond grievance handling and retaliation, we also received suggestions including on workplace harassment issues in the WFL.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In Singapore, we have a multi-pronged approach to address harassment issues, including in the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There are criminal offences under the Protection from Harassment Act and the Penal Code.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We also have a Tripartite Advisory on Managing Workplace Harassment.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The grievance handling processes required under this Bill can also be used by victims of workplace harassment, to surface their cases to employers for resolution.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Beyond this, the tripartite partners have agreed to develop a Tripartite Standard to complement the existing Tripartite Advisory, that will guide and encourage employers to adopt best practices in this area.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This bolsters our educational efforts and complements our current legal protections, to create safer workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What if in spite of all that, the employer and employee are unable to settle their differences within the firm?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: While an employee should first bring up the issue to the firm, not every instance of communication and conciliation within the firm will be successful.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In such cases, the employee can decide if they wish to make a private employment claim under the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will introduce a second Bill later to provide this option for claimants.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today's Bill is the first of two Bills and will cover the substantive rights and obligations under the WFL.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have chosen to introduce it early so that employers can have more time to prepare themselves for the new law.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The second Bill will pertain more specifically to how private employment claims can be made for workplace discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It will take us some time to work through the details, which are complex and novel, on how such claims are adjudicated.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But let me give Members a preview and share the broad approach towards private claims, which was recommended by the Tripartite Committee.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: As with all employment disputes, adjudication is a last resort.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This preserves a non-litigious culture, encourages open communication and trust and achieves better outcomes for everyone.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Today, the Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT) already hears employment claims, such as for wrongful dismissals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It adopts a judge-led approach focused on resolving the dispute quickly, privately and amicably.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are studying how we can empower the ECT to hear workplace discrimination claims with the same principles as far as possible, while deterring frivolous and vexatious claims against employers with the appropriate safeguards.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will educate on what is discrimination, what is not discrimination, such as when language proficiency is a business requirement, and what to do where there is discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will illustrate with examples and provide accessible channels of advice and support.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Most employers are responsible and comply with TGFEP.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: They will not see a heavy increase in their obligations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The WFL is not about making it more difficult or burdensome for these employers or companies to operate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Instead, what it does is that it provides employers with greater certainty on the rules and expectations, so that they know how to act.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: On the education and capability building front, TAFEP is working closely with partners like SNEF, the Institute for Human Resource Professionals (IHRP), the Singapore Human Resources Institute and the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: TAFEP has set up a one-stop resource webpage for employers, employees and HR professionals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There will also be briefings, clinics and webinars, including those catered to small and medium enterprises (SMEs).

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: MOM will continue to support firms on this journey by helping employers that may be in breach of the WFL to understand their obligations and to rectify the breach.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In line with our educational approach, we will provide time for employers to prepare themselves for the new legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is why we have chosen to introduce this first Bill earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We also recognise that small firms may have limited capabilities and resources, and that this can make full compliance from day one difficult.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will review this in five years after the law is implemented.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In the meantime, the TGFEP will continue to apply to these small firms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, it does not mean that we are going to tolerate discrimination because the same guidelines within the TGFEP will continue to apply to these small firms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Part 7 provides calibrated levers that balance between effective deterrence and rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For less severe breaches, these include directions to attend educational workshops and administrative financial penalties imposed by MOM.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For the more severe breaches, MOM can bring the offenders to Court to recommend heavier civil penalties.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: To be clear, there are enforcement actions that the Government can take, which are in addition to the private claims that employees can make.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: (In Mandarin):   Our current fair and harmonious workplace norms did not come by easily.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Therefore, the Workplace Fairness Bill will protect these norms.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have considered the experiences of other countries and recognise the complexity of introducing this legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Protecting workplace and social harmony requires striking an appropriate balance to avoid creating a litigious culture in the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It provides an additional layer of protection to ensure employers evaluate and hire employees fairly based on work capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Bill will also stipulate protective measures for handling disputes, allowing employees to report discriminatory behaviours without fear.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: For businesses, the Bill ensures that employers can make hiring decisions based on genuine business needs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This includes considering whether job applicants can fulfil job responsibilities.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Employers may also decide not to hire certain employees for health and safety reasons or regulatory requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: There is an old saying, "The law is not separate from human sentiment", meaning that legal principles must be established according to common sense and human nature.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We understand that most employers adopt fair employment practices and understand the importance of a harmonious workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Therefore, after the new Bill takes effect, we will adopt an education-first approach, guiding employers to correct their behaviour rather than imposing penalties immediately.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Only employers who commit serious violations will face fines or be prosecuted in Court.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Minister, you are almost reaching your speech limit.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: If you are going to stretch it a bit more, I will ask the Deputy Leader to raise the Motion.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not know whether I will exceed the five minutes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: After studying the experiences in other countries, we recognise the complexities in introducing such laws.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We want to preserve our hard-earned harmony in the workplace and in society.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We also do not want to make the workplace a litigious environment.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This law also ensures that employers retain the flexibility to make decisions based on genuine business needs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we will afford religious groups some flexibility to make employment decisions based on religion.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Meanwhile, we will preserve the common space for secular jobs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We recognise that most employers have adopted fair employment practices and want to do the right thing.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It will encourage an atmosphere of trust and openness where issues on workplace discrimination can be raised safely and resolved amicably.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In doing so, we aim to preserve, we aim to reinforce and to improve our existing workplace norms on fair and harmonious workplaces.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Beyond the WFL and TGFEP, we need to cultivate the right mindsets and a shared understanding that everyone benefits from a fairer workplace.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The tripartite partners are committed to continuing our efforts at nurturing these mindsets and norms in the workplaces and beyond.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We welcome everyone to join us in this whole-of-society effort to build fairer and more harmonious workplaces together.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Before I call the first speaker to kick off the debate, Deputy Leader, would you like to move the Motion on Exempted Business?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, and for some years now, several Members of Parliament on both sides of the House have also called for such legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But as late as 2018, MOM spoke out against the codification of the Tripartite Guidelines for Fair Employment Practices into legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It argued that doing so would not lead to superior employment outcomes and, separately, that the specific anti-discrimination legislation may have the unintended consequence of deterring businesses from hiring workers because these businesses would become fearful of dismissing workers without legitimate reasons.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I spoke at some length about the importance of such legislation in my first speech as Leader of the Opposition in 2020 during the debate after the opening of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This Bill sends a fundamental and powerful message.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It speaks to how the state deals with where Singaporeans stand at workplaces in their own country.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It speaks to how the state recognises multi-racialism, especially when minorities form about 25% of the population.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a powerful signal, particularly when one considers the domestic context over the last decades.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would include the fears of some Singaporeans becoming second class citizens in their own country, where some believe job prospects are better if you are a foreigner on an Employment Pass (EP) than a local born or naturalised Singaporean.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I will speak on some issues the Bill raises and seek clarifications on some others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues, Sylvia Lim, He Ting Ru, Faisal Manap and Louis Chua will also speak on this important Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, on clause 3, which covers the purpose of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It states four purposes to this proposed legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Second, it establishes fair employment practices, including the codification of the Fair Employment Framework and legislating how employers handle grievances.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Where does this Bill leave foreigners who are critical complementary components in many sectors of the economy?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Bill correctly offers wide and significant protections to them as well, notwithstanding clause 22.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is a simple exception, worded in the negative but clear in its intent.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Employers should always aim to recruit Singaporeans and PRs first.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Otherwise, how do we build and sustain a united people and nation heavily reliant on immigration, which is a fault line in many parts of the world?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How do we convince Singaporeans that their National Service commitments are not in vain?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How do we convince them that the state will always have their backs?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Hence, employers should not see this legislation just as an administrative process, or worse, a burden.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would even go so far as to say that it is a critical piece of legislation with a view towards nation building in the years to come, where many of our challenges will be domestic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It covers discrimination, not just with respect to hiring decisions but to in-employment decisions, such as performance appraisals, promotions, training opportunities and finally, dismissals.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the protected characteristics or the specific discriminatory grounds set out, Part 3 of the Bill seeks to define the meaning of eight out of 11 characteristics.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clauses 9 to 16 seek to clarify the ambit of these characteristics and must be read with exceptions at Part 5 to be properly contextualised and understood by workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Employers are allowed to consider a discriminatory hire if there are genuine job requirements on the grounds of age, in favour of citizens and PRs, on religious grounds and on grounds of disability.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the main, the exceptions are fair and practical and they provide significant operating space for employers to make employment decisions in the best interest of their corporate entities and companies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, I found the explanatory statement to clause 17(3) intuitively problematic and odd, especially since this Bill addresses discrimination.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What has the race of A's husband got to do with A's employment and dismissal?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: By extension, other extreme examples that would not be out of place here would be when A chooses to fire the worker if the worker's spouse is a foreigner, or their parents are too old, or the child or A's child is mentally disabled.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These examples show how mind-boggling discrimination by association can be insofar as the explanatory statement is concerned.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Minister clarify what this clause seeks to achieve in favour of an employer with concrete examples from TAFEP's history, given that TAFEP has been around for close to 20 years?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These examples may be more useful than explaining what is sought to be achieved by this clause.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Workers must note that for practical purposes, they would need to secure evidence to lodge a workplace fairness claim.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note the Tripartite Committee's Workplace Fairness legislation final report which listed two key requirements to that end.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: First, the claimant or the worker should clearly cite the incident that led him or her to believe that he or she suffered an adverse employment outcome because of a protected characteristic, and the cited incident should show how the consideration of the discriminatory action, for example, on the grounds of age or nationality led to that adverse employment outcome.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The report also says that documentary evidence, such as emails, mobile phone messages and oral testimonies, which are signed by witnesses, will strengthen the claim.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These requirements are likely to be a bridge too far for many workers, and discriminations on the grounds of the protected characteristics may be quite difficult to prove, particularly at the moment of employment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I would be grateful if the Minister could share some examples of how TAFEP helped workers who made such complaints on the grounds of nationality and age at the moment of employment, were successfully resolved.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I choose nationality and age because these are the two characteristics which rank highest in terms of complaints by workers on the grounds.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These examples would help workers appreciate the evidentiary threshold that has to be overcome to succeed in a claim.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the Tripartite Committee's report does list out some helpful examples that would be useful to guide workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the absence of illustrations in the Bill, it would be important for these examples to be profiled and updated, as appropriate, on easily accessible public resources on a public service website or channel, not just for the convenience of workers and employees, but for a more realistic understanding of what is perceived to be discrimination as envisaged by this legislation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The fact that not all the illustrations in the Committee's report are automatically determinative of discrimination is a reminder that proving workplace discrimination is not always straightforward and many workers will also have to be alive to the reality of indirect discrimination.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The prospect of indirect discrimination was raised by my colleague Sengkang Group Representation Constituency (GRC) Member of Parliament Ms He Ting Ru in a Parliamentary Question (PQ) in 2023.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Bill before the House does not cover indirect discrimination as the Tripartite Committee opined that it would impose very wide legal obligations on employers, resulting in uncertainty for both employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, there was a concern of an overly legalistic relationship between employer and employee.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While this perspective is not completely without merit, it must be remembered there could be some cases of employment decisions that arise out of norms, culture or processes that are nonetheless discriminatory.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This would be one area to monitor closely going forward to better support workers who are commonly in a more inferior bargaining position compared to their bosses and employers, who exert significant control over them.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note that TAFEP will welcome complaints covering indirect discrimination, even if this Bill does not list indirect discrimination as a protected characteristic.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To complement the Bill, it would be critical for TAFEP to list out examples of such indirect discrimination going forward, which it should profile publicly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleagues, Sengkang GRC Members of Parliament, Ms He Ting Ru and Mr Louis Chua will speak on the development of the common law with regard to indirect discrimination in other jurisdictions, which have a longer history of hosting anti-discrimination legislation to better address such problems.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: They will also speak on the important subject of reasonable accommodations, including for workers who are differently abled.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleague, Ms Sylvia Lim, will speak on this issue of timing and other matters in her speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This exemption was the subject matter of my PQ to MOM in 2023, when I enquired how many discrimination-related complaints were made by workers and employees working in companies with a headcount of less than 25.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is not an insignificant number and I have some queries in this regard.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: More significantly, as provided for in clause 28, the Bill provides not insignificant protection for workers when they raise grievances to the employer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In view of the protections available for workers who make legitimate claims and the prospect of other civil relief which will be made known by the Government later in the year through sister legislation, I hope more resources can be placed at the feet of these smaller companies to help them come up to speed with the requirements of this legislation by way of regular updates from TAFEP, so that all workers can be covered by this anti-discrimination law in good time.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I note Minister, in his opening speech to this Bill, stressed about various educational resources that will be developed, so I take the point that the Minister raised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I understand and respect the approach of the tripartite partners in taking a staggered approach out of practical necessity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, a clear roadmap with intermediate goals towards compliance for companies with less than 25 workers would be necessary as the Bill today still does not cover 25% of our workforce.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For many Singaporeans, work takes up a significant part of almost all our lives.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In a recent podcast last month, the Prime Minister, Mr Lawrence Wong, remarked, and I quote, "In any multiracial society, it is harder to be a minority than the majority." The Prime Minister urged those in the majority community to be sensitive, engaged and to reach out to minorities across all aspects of life.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These remarks are relevant to the Bill before the House and promotes the outcomes that this Bill seeks.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, workers need to consider that some employers' perceived lack of sensitivity may be down to ignorance, inexperience and a lack of exposure, as opposed to malice.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For things to change, greater professionalism and mutual respect at the workplace must be promoted.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such HR improvements welcomed through open conversations can boost productivity, if sincerely undertaken by both workers and employers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: My colleague, Aljunied GRC Member of Parliament, Mr Faisal Manap, will speak on this point from a different perspective, with a view to engender greater understanding for some of our workers and compromise from employers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For small and medium enterprises (SMEs) with less than 25 employees that professionalise more swiftly and adopt workplace fairness practices and are ready before the five-year exemption period is over, such workplaces may well generate greater interest from jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A fair workplace-ready TAFEP accreditation scheme for workplaces with less than 25 employees may well be something the Ministry can consider as an intermediate option before the review of the applicability of this legislation for these companies comes up.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I hope the Government can pay close attention to the processes by which these smaller companies currently not covered by the Bill are educated about their obligations under the TGFEP after this Bill is passed, with a view to their prospective coverage under the Bill in future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Next, on administrative penalties, clause 31 details the administrative penalties that will be invoked when employers are issued with a contravention notice, requiring them to pay an administrative penalty of the prescribed amount.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The nature of the civil contraventions is wide, ranging from penalties for retaliation against complainants to the publication of a discriminatory direction to providing inaccurate particulars to the Commissioner, amongst others.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the Minister can provide some clarity with respect to the dollar value of the administrative penalties under clause 31(a) to (i).

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Clause 34(1) devolves significant powers to the Commissioner to determine what constitutes a serious civil contravention by the use of the term, and I quote, "whenever it appears".

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can I confirm if these powers relate directly to what has been established as serious civil contraventions in clause 30, or are there other serious civil contraventions which are contemplated and not captured by the Bill?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, some guidance and clarity as to what these are would be useful and stated for the record.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Bill requires workers to go for compulsory mediation before considering the prospect of legal recourse, ostensibly with a view to maintain harmonious industrial relations and to avoid a litigious culture.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The legal process and legal proceedings would reveal the identity of the companies that commit such egregious discrimination or serious civil contraventions.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this extent, is it the intention of the Bill for the Commissioner to also reveal the names and circumstances of companies that are subject to administrative penalties as envisaged under clause 31?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: TAFEP has hitherto been conservative in revealing the names of companies found to have fallen foul of their fair employment practices.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Naming the employers who fall foul of this Bill is not to encourage a name and shame culture.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: On the contrary, such an approach would be useful in supporting the purposes of the Bill, educating companies and workers at large about discriminatory practices at the workplace and to nudge employers to always take workplace discrimination very seriously to the benefit of workers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After all, the only natural resource of Singapore is our human resource and it is in our interest as a nation to ensure that all our workers receive protection from discrimination.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The WP will debate this separately at its Second Reading.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is assumed that this will give better options for workers to pursue claims against unscrupulous employers.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I look forward to the Minister's responses to my clarifications.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I congratulate our tripartite partners, various stakeholders and the Attorney-General's Chambers for working tirelessly over three years to see to the introduction of this Bill and its Second Reading today.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I rise in strong support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I have raised in this House, since my maiden speech in Parliament in 2011, on this issue and the need to strengthen the Singaporean core and ensuring workers, especially professionals, managers and executives (PMEs), have a level-playing field.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Since then, we have, in the past decade, introduced a compendium of legislative changes, tripartite guidelines and tripartite advisories, including new policies and now, this Bill, to address this.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It has been some years since I suggested introducing some form of workplace anti-discrimination law.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This call was echoed during NTUC's engagements with more than 10,000 PMEs, employers and stakeholders through the joint NTUC-SNEF PME Taskforce from 2020 to 2021, which I co-chaired with SNEF.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For more than a decade, I have received numerous letters, emails and messages as well as have had many coffee sessions with PMEs of various ages across different organisational levels and in different industries to hear their woes, frustrations and anxieties.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This Bill will answer the Labour Movement's long and consistent calls to ensure fair access to good work opportunities for our workers, especially PMEs.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It would confer protection for the most common types of discrimination faced by workers today and our unions will now be able to better protect our members through the expanded suite of individual remedies and calibrated penalties for discriminatory employment practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: All said, the success of this Bill will depend on five key factors which I call the five "C"s: coverage, clarity, communication, capability and complement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is important that this piece of legislation will cover the majority and most common forms of workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Labour Movement believes that no form of discrimination should be tolerated at the workplace.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Workers must be treated fairly, based on merit, and we want to see that employers do not run afoul of this new law.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Besides the protected characteristics, there may be fewer common areas not explicitly covered, such as sexual orientation and gender identity or expression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Even if not covered by the new legislation, an employer who runs afoul of the TGFEP must be subjected to investigation and enforcement actions and measures by MOM and TAFEP.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By the same token, MOM has planned to exempt smaller companies from this Bill for a start.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I humbly submit that all companies and employers should be subjected to this new piece of legislation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Aside from giving more time for SMEs to prepare and comply with this new legislation, companies should not be exonerated from such responsibilities by virtue of size indefinitely.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: SMEs, like larger companies, have an equal responsibility to foster a fair and inclusive workplace for their workers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: During my ground engagements, I also realised that outsourced workers and freelancers, including platform workers, may be an underserved worker segment in this space.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I envisage they should, similarly, be protected against discrimination in the course of their work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: However, as this is the first iteration of the workplace fairness legislation, I submit that, after passing as law, the legislation should undergo timely and regular reviews in keeping with possible changes in societal and social norms, in and outside the workplace and a changing workforce profile.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This constant and careful review of coverage and exemptions is imperative to ensure no genuine victim of discrimination will be left in the lurch.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The Labour Movement will continue to listen closely to workers’ feedback and lobby for further changes to the workplace fairness legislation, even after it is implemented, to ensure its relevancy and cater to the needs, expectations and conditions of workers and the world of work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There has been much discussion on the topic of what is fair and what is discrimination, whether the law should cover both direct and indirect discrimination; and what evidence needs to be produced to prove and substantiate a claim by a claimant or complainant.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And for the protected characteristics, whether disability covers mental disability and, if so, to what extent?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These are pertinent questions which should be exhaustively articulated in the legislation if not otherwise, through the relevant advisories, guidelines, illustrations or frequently asked questions issued by our tripartite partners in a clear and succinct manner.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will provide clarity and certainty to HR, employment and industrial relations practitioners, lawyers and in-house counsels, unions, union leaders and employers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This will further eradicate frivolous or speculative claims in addition to those already provided.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: By the same token and for greater clarity, I have a number of clarifications regarding the Bill, which I will go in order of the clause numbers for easier reference by Members of the House.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In clause 5(2), "asking for information or documents… for purposes of possible employment" is part of an employment decision.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In job application forms, would employers have to remove fields asking for protected characteristics, such as age, race, sex and so on?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Will job candidates also have the right to reject providing this information, on the basis that it will "adversely affect" them, as defined in clause 17?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Clarity is important because if the maximum age for who is deemed to be an infant is too low, a female worker may lose her protection when breastfeeding an older child.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Clause 18 covers discrimination by employers' direction, instruction or policy published in writing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: The existence of such directions, instructions or policies may be substantiated by evidence, for example, witnesses' testimonies, and as currently worded, employers may get around clause 18 by not putting things in writing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Clause 19 prohibits discrimination by published advertisements or description.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: But employers can also discriminate by asking questions about protected characteristics during the job application process, even when not justified by any genuine occupational requirements.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Clause 20(2)(a) provides an exception if the nature of the job means it cannot be "reasonably performed by an individual unless the individual has (or does not have) the protected characteristic".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This is likely to be the most widely used exception and I would call for clear guidance to prevent abuse.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, if some employees of the employer can only speak proficiently in a particular language, will proficiency of that language be regarded as reasonably necessary for the performance of the job, as otherwise communication would not be possible?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, can strong preferences by customers be considered reasonably necessary for the performance of the job?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: For example, parents strongly preferring female early childhood educators at kindergartens or female tutors at tuition centres to teach their young children.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As the young pupils would be of different sexes, the preservation of modesty exception would not apply.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, given that it is crucial for there not only to be a grievance handling policy, but one that works well in practice, what are the safeguards in the law to ensure that employers not only have written policies but also abide by them in practice?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Put in another way, what recourse do workers have if they are dissatisfied with how their grievances were handled?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, under what circumstances would it be "reasonably necessary" for an employer to disclose victims' identity and the inquiry details to any person, with reference to clause 27(e)?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Clause 28 prohibits employers from taking any retaliatory action against employees who raise grievances or pursue claims under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I am heartened that the prohibition against retaliation also includes workplace harassment grievances.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Second, not offering re-employment is an adverse employment decision only if it is attributable to retaliation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In other cases where the employer did not offer re-employment, the affected employees can make representations to the Minister under the Retirement and Re-employment Act.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In those other cases, would evidence of discrimination by the employer be relevant?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Third, would protections against retaliation by employers on the basis of grievances covered by the TGFEP levers be similarly strengthened for parity with the provisions on prohibition against retaliation under this new Workplace Fairness legislation?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Small companies, with fewer than 25 employees, who are exempted from the Workplace Fairness legislation should be held accountable for any retaliatory acts against their employees who report discrimination under TGFEP.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Looking at clause 35(2), it appears that some cases may be regarded as both civil contraventions and serious civil contraventions.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Last clarification, in making a complaint to MOM for employers' discrimination, could the Minister give guidance on what type of relevant evidence would workers need to produce or show before MOM will investigate further?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: This landmark legislation will cover much ground and its effective implementation and enforcement will not be easy or straightforward.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: At the onset, there will be questions from all quarters.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: These questions are opportunities to sharpen our approach and build trust and unity among all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is, therefore, imperative that we address all concerns and commence communication about this new law and how it will eventually be operationalised at the earliest opportunity.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: It is my hope that the nuts and bolts can be well cascaded to every employer as well as every union, union leader, HR and legal practitioner and every worker operating in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Communication can come in various forms and channels, such as a legal handbook, pocket series or guide, or even a dedicated website with an exhaustive deck of frequently asked questions, coupled with legal primers catered to the various levels of needs and segments.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: To enhance workplace fairness and the knowledge in this space, more can be done to improve HR capabilities as well as workplace practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Echoing the recommendations in the PME Taskforce Report, there is a need to improve HR standards and increase take-up of IHRP certification.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We need this Bill to complement existing legislation and other worker protections.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: In short, we need to create a safer environment for workers to report discriminatory practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Despite the increased availability of formal grievance-handling procedures, workers may not feel safe enough to do so.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: According to the report, the main reason was the fear of being marginalised at work or making work relations awkward.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I submit that this is where unions can play a crucial role in supporting our members.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Our union leaders are trusted and experienced peers and advocates who understand the challenges our members face and are trained to provide relevant support and advice.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Indeed, there are many overlaps between harassment and discrimination.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I have, in the past, made repeated calls to address workplace harassment.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: All of us – workers, employers and members of society – will need to play our part to achieve this vision.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: True progress requires a collective commitment to check our own biases at work, practice inclusion and speak up when we spot that something is not right.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: There are available avenues to seek redress and NTUC, together with our unions, will continue to do our part to ensure that our workers are protected and have fair opportunities at work to fulfil their potential.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: We stand ready to support our members and workers who face any challenging situations at the workplaces because #everyworkermatters.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The WP 2020 manifesto calls for explicit anti-discrimination legislation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is because we felt that TAFEP guidelines and enforcement via restriction of access to work permits were not enough to stamp out discriminatory practices.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Moreover, we believe that formal legislation would provide clarity for both employers and employees, and Singaporeans in general, because laws do not just provide mechanisms, but are also signals of our society's generally accepted moral intuitions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Then-Minister for Manpower Josephine Teo said in September 2020, that it might not result in better employment outcomes for vulnerable groups and asked if we might be more interested in form or substance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The second part of the speech will cover what I believe to be a clear and major gap in the Bill – discrimination via denial of reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: On non-workplace discrimination, I understand that this may feel novel in the Singapore context, but are we simply taking a conservative approach to deciding and prioritising practicable applications of anti-discrimination legislation?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Is the Government exploring whether it can legislate against significant and harmful discrimination in interactions that bear similar dynamics to employment, such as in the use of private and public services.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For instance, the purchasing of goods and services on gig work platforms could be a scenario where discrimination takes place.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Should landlords be allowed to discriminate against those from a certain racial background or a specific family size?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The United Kingdom (UK) Equality Act specifically prohibits discrimination in the provision of services in access to premises and education.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And while of course we do not advocate the wholesale copying of such laws, nor do we claim that these other jurisdictions are utopias without their problems, it seems a missed opportunity for us to legislate to outlaw discriminatory practices more generally.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: However, could the Minister clarify if the Government sees the lack of coverage of indirect discrimination as a problem and how would we effectively address what some might call nationality-based discrimination against Singaporean workers?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, it is often a practical impossibility to prove such alleged nationality discrimination.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Workers are often only able to cite anecdotes about foreign HR managers being biased towards candidates or colleagues from their own country, while statistics showing larger than proportionate representation from some countries can be brushed off as coincidence.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: While the Tripartite Guidelines do mention that employers should not suggest preference based on National Service liabilities, it is unclear whether they can ask about PES status.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: PES status can, after all, be used as a blunt tool to assess if the job applicant may have a medical condition or neurodivergent condition.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Again, indirect discrimination is prohibited in several other developed jurisdictions like the UK, and indeed, their Equality Act was considered in the Tripartite Committee's review.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Are such claims really that complex to introduce legislation for?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And if prohibiting indirect discrimination is meant to be left covered by TAFEP guidelines, when will these guidelines be made available?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: After all, our society appreciates that indirect discrimination is unacceptable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For example, there was a significant public outcry after a hijab wearing Muslim worker was asked to remove her hijab in order to work as a promoter at a departmental store just a few years ago.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is a classic example of indirect discrimination, where a neutral policy about uniform and appropriate dress disproportionately affects certain groups, in this case, Muslim women.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Another example of indirect discrimination in a disability context is a requirement for candidates to participate in a phone interview for a data entry role.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This requirement disproportionately affects deaf and mute candidates who are not able to complete the phone interview satisfactorily and are disqualified as a result.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such cases are precisely why indirect discrimination is recognised and regulated in many developed jurisdictions, including the UK, the European Union (EU) and Australia.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Our Bill, however, remains silent on this front, which will permit covert biases to continue unaddressed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: We should not under-estimate the significance of closing this gap.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Those who rely on statutory protections are often the most vulnerable segments of our workforce – employees with disabilities, lower-income workers, older workers, women who juggle caregiving responsibilities and those who start with less advantage in working life.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If we only address blatant overt acts of discrimination, we inadvertently leave behind these hidden or systemic patterns, which can be just as corrosive to social harmony and economic security.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Next, several characteristics that are well-known sources of discrimination are also not covered by the Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: For instance, those who have chronic medical conditions, like arthritis and regular migraines, are not covered.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It also appears that the Bill's coverage of intellectual disabilities appears to indicate that learning disabilities are not included.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I based this on SG Enable's definition of intellectual disability as mainly established by a person having an intelligence quotient of 70 and below, or a feature of medical conditions, like Down syndrome, which is quite different from learning disabilities, such as dyslexia, which the Dyslexia Association of Singapore estimates to affect around 10 percent of the population in Singapore.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity are also explicitly excluded in the Bill, which seems at odds with the Minister for Home Affairs' statements that gay people deserve dignity, respect, acceptance and do not deserve to be stigmatised because of their sexual orientation during his opening speech in 2022, when this House debated the repeal of section 377A of the Penal Code and attendant amendments to the Constitution.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is notable as researchers as at organisations, such as National University of Singapore's Saw Swee Hock School of Public Health and the Association of Women for Action and Research (AWARE) have found that more than half of LGBTQ persons have experienced discrimination at the workplace and that levels are generally higher than those who do not identify as LGBTQ.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This concern about employment has also been raised by LGBTQ individuals to party colleagues, previously sharing that they have experienced discrimination from employers who declined to hire them on the grounds of their sexual orientation.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: This is disturbing, as we should aim to harness the contributions of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Even if we are not to include these characteristics in the legislation, I would like to seek clarification from the Minister about how the Ministry plans to address such types of discrimination experienced by fellow Singaporeans, particularly, as it is not currently explicitly covered by TAFEP guidelines.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Fourthly, I would like the Government to clarify why they and the Tripartite Committee excluded large classes of workers from coverage under the Bill.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: It is also not a novel point of law, with many developed jurisdictions and international law to take reference from.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, these decisions must have been deliberate, and the Government should be open with why they were taken.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: I am not casting aspersions, but I hope that we can have better clarity and understanding of the thought process and timing behind how the Government intends to ensure that these groups too, are eventually afforded legal protections against discriminatory behaviour.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Reasonable accommodations are necessary, appropriate and practical adjustments made to a job to make it fairer and more accessible to people with disabilities (PwDs), with the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (UNCRPD) definition, highlighting that the point is to ensure they can exercise all human rights and fundamental freedoms on an equal basis with others.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Singapore is a party to the CRPD, where states recognise the need to protect the provision of reasonable accommodations, and said they would take all appropriate steps to ensure their provision.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
