text: The Minister mentioned that tripartite partners are working on advisory on the provision of reasonable accommodations for PwDs, and as of May 2024, the Government's view is that the difficulty in clearly defining what constitutes reasonable accommodations could result in heavy litigation, citing what has happened in some other countries.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: But disability advocates have highlighted that reasonable accommodations are by far their number one hurdle when it comes to employment.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: They are essential to PwDs participating in the workforce.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Considering that the Government has tabled the Workplace Fairness Bill today and acknowledge the lack of teeth of tough-help guidelines, what recourse can PwDs expect if their employers fail or refuse to comply with the tripartite advisory when these come into play?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: As a matter of international law, does the Government consider Singapore to be compliant with our obligations under the CRPD if we do not legally recognise a right to reasonable accommodations?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: If so, how does it reconcile its position with the views on the UNCRPD to the contrary?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Could this mean developing policy mechanisms with a carrot-and-stick approach for employers to provide reasonable accommodations, such as outlined below?

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Employers should be convinced about the value of having a genuine interactive process upon receiving any request for accommodation, something which has already been introduced in December 2024, with the flexi-work arrangements (FWAs).

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Like FWA request, this will entail timely acknowledgement of employer requests and good faith aspiration of workable solutions.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: When a request is deemed impractical, an employer should be required to provide written explanations of proposed alternatives.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Such a mutual dialogue builds trust, helps mitigate disputes and ensures that both parties collaborate to arrive at sensible balanced arrangements.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Establishing what is undue hardship for employers will also be helpful in guiding employers as to when a requested accommodation becomes unworkable.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Factors, such as employer size, resources and potential operation impact must be taken into account and should also take into account existing subsidies or supportive programmes.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: In the meantime, the upcoming advisory should also be made as effective as possible with concrete plans for uptake, targeting companies and industries which are the least likely to be providing reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: That advisory must not just be preaching to the converted.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: The advisory should also have a basic definition of what a reasonable accommodation is, taking guidance from the UNCRPD that Singapore has ratified.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: And if people lose faith that this legislation can protect them, a deeper disillusionment sets in where they feel that systemic inequalities cannot be solved.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Any subpar results may ironically confirm the Government's prior argument that legislation might be only formed.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: So, we must ensure it has real substance.

speaker: Ms He Ting Ru (Sengkang)
text: Only then can we confidently say that we have a Workplace Fairness Act that is both firm in principle and forceful in practice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This challenge will be heightened by our growing demographic shift toward an ageing population and if age discrimination is not adequately addressed, it could have serious economic and social implications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Recent reports indicate that age discrimination is not only present in our labour market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The stickiness in age bias indicates that there are older workers who will continue to face barriers in accessing good job opportunities and prospects on a fair basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This issue would be particularly pertinent in industries where experience and expertise are highly valued and where older workers still find themselves sidelined in favour of younger candidates.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The struggle is especially evident in PME workers who are in their 40s and 50s.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These workers often report that their age is viewed as a disadvantage and it limits their in-employment prospects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: A survey conducted by NTUC found that 60% of older workers surveyed felt they were discriminated against when it came to training opportunities, with younger workers receiving priority for consideration for upgrading and upskilling programmes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This gap in access to opportunities for growth and development across because of age is not trivial.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The effects of age discrimination extend beyond individual workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The ageing population is one of the most significant challenges facing global economies today.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: As populations age, fewer young workers enter the workforce while more older workers reach the end of their work lives, they retire, leading to a declining labour force participation rate.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: In our case in Singapore, for example, our labour force participation rate has shown a small, gradual decline, for example, over the last three years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This demographic trend is expected to limit workforce growth, exacerbating the challenges of economic sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Older workers represent a critical component of the workforce.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: However, when ageism hinders their employment opportunities, wages and career progression, it not only impacts individual workers but also reduces the overall productivity potential of the economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: An Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) study has shown that an age-diverse workforce actually offers a larger set of skills and enhances organisational sustainability and profitability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: By excluding older workers from the labour force or by not giving them fair opportunities due to age bias, businesses miss out on valuable experience and expertise that can help drive growth and innovation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Furthermore, with the increasing rate of job turnover, especially in sectors like informcomms technology and financial services, mid-career workers are especially vulnerable to age discrimination.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Even not-so-old workers, like those retrenched in their 40s or 50s from these industries, may struggle to find new employment opportunities due to biases in recruitment and hiring practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This not only affects the workers but also their families, as they face what could be prolonged periods of unemployment or under-employment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: To address these issues, it is important that our legislative frameworks evolve to offer stronger protection against age discrimination and promote age fairness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I therefore welcome the introduction of the Workplace Fairness Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This Bill marks a significant step in the fight against workplace discrimination, including workplace ageism, in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I am glad that this point is acknowledged on both sides of the House.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: This legislative clarity sends a clear signal and message that age discrimination will not be tolerated and that every worker, regardless of age, deserves equitable opportunities in the workforce and in the workplace.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For instance, employers can give preferential treatment to senior workers in hiring decisions, which can be particularly beneficial in addressing the challenges of an ageing population.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The WFL, together with other age-friendly laws, such as the Retirement and Re-employment Act will further strengthen the advocacy and realisation of equitable protection of the rights of older workers vis-a-vis their younger counterparts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: While legal protections are essential, they are not sufficient in their own to eliminate ageism or, as the Minister puts it, it is not a panacea.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Together with the law, it is critical that organisations also adopt age-friendly workplace practices that promote inclusion and provide equal opportunities for workers of all ages.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: FWAs is one of the common ways in which employers can accommodate the needs of older workers, allowing them to remain productive and engaged in the workforce longer, while simultaneously facilitating succession and renewal for the organisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: A joint study conducted in 2023 by NTUC with the Singapore University of Social Sciences and Tsao Foundation revealed that nearly half of the employers surveyed said that they had implemented such practices to extend the employment of their older workers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: These flexible arrangements help to mitigate the challenges that come with ageing, such as physical limitations or caregiving responsibilities and allow workers to continue contributing their skills and expertise to the organisation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Additionally, job redesign is another key area where employers can create more inclusive workplaces.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Age-friendly job design takes into account the needs and capabilities of older workers and provides them with the tools and resources necessary to succeed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For example, companies can offer training programmes to help older workers develop new skills, especially in areas like digital literacy, which is critical in today's rapidly evolving job market.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: The recruitment stage is also an area that employers must be vigilant about to carefully examine the tools they use in recruitment and hiring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: For example, on top of potential human biases, in other words, the interviewers, you can also see that companies might increasingly make use of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in their hiring processes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: Age discrimination undermines the potential of older workers and the broader economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: By strengthening and systematically promoting age fairness and tackling ageism resolutely, we can help ensure that older workers are given the respect and opportunities they deserve and that businesses can benefit from the wealth of experience and knowledge that they bring to the table.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: But at the same time, I think we should pay good attention to the name of this Bill and I think it is core intent – which is fairness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: And I think there is a difference between just acting against discrimination as against, also focusing enough attention on promoting and operationalising fairness.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Defence (Mr Heng Chee How)
text: I think those two must go hand-in-hand in terms of how we can get the best out of our workforce and how we can leverage our strong tripartite relationship and industrial harmony to do the best for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sorry, Mr Faisal Manap, could you just take a seat first?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But for the purpose of WFL, for the purpose of this Bill, as I have alluded to the journey that we have taken for the last many years, the fact that so many people have come up and we have taken all of their considerations, to move it to a more surefooted way of crafting a Bill, we wanted to be very well-scoped in terms of defining what the definition of this protected characteristic is and what does the protected characteristic cover.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But that does not mean that, moving forward, we would not continue to review.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because it is a live document, we will continue to get data, to look at where the areas of needs are and we will continue to improve that and expand the coverage itself.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that can correct, in case the Member has any misperception.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The issue I had was specifically with clause 17(3) and the way it has been drafted in the explanatory statement.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I am not going to repeat my speech.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: If I recall correctly, in my speech, I sought clarity on examples which would show why clause 17(3) would be important for an employer.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What I am suggesting is the explanation on clause 17(3) and the explanatory statement of the Bill on page 44, to me, sounds intuitively odd.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: It would be helpful, through the experience of TAFEP, if the Minister could share, perhaps, later, in the round-up speech, examples of why this particular clause is important and is to be included in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: That would be helpful, so we can understand the clause better.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We, indeed, will cover that in my wrap-up speech.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not want to belabour the point because we are only at the beginning.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I note the fact that there is significant interest.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the record, I thank the Leader of the Opposition for your support of the Bill at just the Second Reading itself.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I want to, not to belabour the point, the illustration in the explanatory statement was actually taken out of context.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is meant to clarify what is discrimination as defined in the Bill – in this particular Bill itself.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: It is not what we consider to be discrimination in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I cannot emphasise and reiterate more, that we do not tolerate any form of racism and we do not tolerate any form of workplace discrimination.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Like I said, TAFEP will continue to be there.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not want to belabour the point.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The Workers' Party has long voiced the need for legislation to address the issue of workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I will share two scenarios that have been experienced by Singaporean Muslim individuals and would like to seek clarification and confirmation that, based on this bill, discriminatory practices indeed occur in these two scenarios and that the affected individuals can file a report.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The first scenario concerns the observance of Friday prayers for Muslim men.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In general, many Government agencies and employers in the private sector allow Muslim men to perform Friday prayers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, there are still some or a few who do not permit it.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The issue of granting permission to perform Friday prayers was previously raised by former Member of Parliament Mr Zainal Sapari through his social media platform.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari's sharing on this matter was covered by online media outlet Mothership on 17 July 2019, titled "MP Zainal Bin Sapari suggests S'pore employers give Muslim men time-off for Friday Mosque prayers".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Mr Zainal Sapari, who is currently the Assistant Secretary-General of the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC), said he had been approached by Muslim male employees who face difficulties in getting permission from their companies or employers to perform Friday prayers.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: He said that "it would be much appreciated if employers could grant male Muslim workers time-off between 12.30pm to 2.30pm to go to the mosques".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In the same Facebook post, Mr Zainal Sapari also explained the obligation of Friday prayers for Muslim men, and he also opined that "workers should also 'make up for lost company time' by coming to work a little earlier, or leaving later that day".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The second scenario is a situation that has received much attention for a while now, which is the wearing of hijab.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For years, there have been occasional accounts or reports about Muslim women facing situations where they are asked to remove their hijab if they want to be accepted for employment or after they have started work.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This matter was mentioned in the Suara Musyawarah report published in 2013.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This Suara Musyawarah report was produced by an independent and non-partisan committee formed by the government with the objective of gathering feedback as well as concerns and aspirations of the Malay/Muslim community in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: On page 21, paragraph 32 of the Suara Musyawarah report in Malay, and I quote, "This committee has also heard several personal experiences that give the impression that discrimination is also practiced in employment.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Personal examples include employers who clearly state that their preference is for non-Malay workers and Muslim women are sidelined or bluntly told that they are not allowed to wear the hijab".

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In fact, my wife had a similar experience back in 2000 when she was almost accepted to work at a private language centre but with one condition, which was she cannot wear a hijab.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: In this case, as reported in the media, Madam Halimah firmly stated, "there is no place for discrimination of any form and against anyone in Singapore".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I commend the Government and all stakeholders for their efforts in bringing this Bill to fruition.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Workplace Fairness Bill is a significant milestone in promoting fairness and inclusivity in Singapore's employment landscape.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I will focus my remarks, today, on the impact of this Bill on PwDs, drawing on my experience serving this community.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I will also use the terms "disabled", "special needs", "differently abled" interchangeably.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am an activist involved in developing the Enabling Masterplan and initiatives, such as The Purple Parade, The Purple Symphony, and social enterprises, creating jobs for the disabled.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I also head disability charities, such as the Autism Resource Centre, which provides job placement services.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am also the parent of a special needs adult.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I, therefore, will speak from different perspectives, hoping to balance the interests of all stakeholders.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, let me talk about the progress of Singapore's disability landscape Sir, Singapore has made remarkable progress in disability inclusion over the past two decades, thanks to former Prime Minister and current Prime Minister and the Cabinets as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The focus on children with special needs in their early and school years have been transformative over the last two decades.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: These efforts have actually given many families much needed hope and support.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The challenge now is to extend these efforts into adulthood, ensuring that PwDs have meaningful opportunities in the workforce if they can work.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Key initiatives, very well appreciated, included the setting up of the following: SG Enable and its job placement partners, such as SPD, MINDS and the Autism Resource Centre, which have supported over 4,000 job seekers with disabilities through job placement and training programmes.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The Open Door Programme (ODP), which also funds job redesign, workplace modifications and staff training, has benefitted over 400 companies; Special Employment Credit (SEC) and the Job Redesign Grants, which incentivise businesses to hire and accommodate PwDs, have catalysed changes in the corporate sector employment scene; schemes, such as the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS), and other accessibility grants ensure that PwDs also remain engaged in the workforce; and introduced in 2021, the Enabling Mark recognises businesses for their inclusive practices in employment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The latest Enabling Masterplan sets a target to increase this to 40% by 2030.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, I want to thank and congratulate the Government for doing this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But while much has been achieved, there is still significant work to be done.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is about unlocking potential at the individual and societal level.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: With proper training and support, PwDs can contribute meaningfully to workplaces and society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: For PwDs, it is a bridge to inclusion.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is also a bridge to financial independence, allowing them to move beyond being welfare recipients.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Research from the International Labour Organization shows that inclusive workplaces can boost gross domestic product by up to 7%.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Locally, in Singapore, SG Enable's success in matching over 4,000 PwDs with jobs highlights how inclusion enhances economic participation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Companies like UOB, Deutsche Bank and DBS Bank have shown that neurodiverse employees excel in areas, like cybersecurity and digitalisation, proving that inclusion also drives innovation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Now, with Singapore's ageing population and workforce constraints, PwDs represent an untapped talent pool.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: With proper training and support, they can contribute effectively across sectors, from blue-collar to white-collar to silver-collar jobs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Despite its importance, inclusive employment comes with challenges.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Having overseen job training and placement services for PwDs, I have seen both successes and failures.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The key challenges include, one, society's attitudes and bias.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: PwDs are often misunderstood, especially those with non-visible or neurodivergent conditions.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Stigma and lack of awareness hinder their potentials.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Many businesses lack the infrastructure and knowledge to support PwDs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: An SG Enable survey found that over 50% of SMEs perceive hiring PwDs as challenging, due to insufficient accommodations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The third challenge is this, that PwDs themselves have to be ready as well.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: PwDs often require extended training in both vocational and life skills to be adequately prepared for the workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to thank, also, the individuals and organisations who have put in work by stakeholders, such as the PWDs themselves, employers who are enlightened and inclusive, disability organisations, such as Autism Resource Centre, whom I work with, and the Disabled People's Association.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This excludes individuals with learning disabilities, like dyslexia and ADHD, as well as conditions like cerebral palsy, which is more than just a physical disability.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The UNCRPD adopts a broader definition, encompassing all impairments that hinder full participation in society.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Why is broadening the definition of disability for this Bill important?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Individuals, especially those with less-visible disabilities, face significant barriers due to stigma and lack of accommodations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Expanding the definition of disabilities would unlock a broader talent pool, for example, dyslexia, contributing significantly to Singapore's economy.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And that is proposal one: broadening the definition of disability.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Reasonable accommodations, which are, basically, adjustments to the workplace enabling PwDs to perform to their potential, are fundamental to equitable employment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Examples include modifications, like ramps and ergonomic furniture; flexible schedules for medical needs; and assistive technologies, such as screen readers or using visual or appropriate communication methods.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, legislation is necessary to ensure consistency and accountability.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Because mandatory accommodations will support even more PwDs to contribute meaningfully to the workforce.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Successful policies, such as Singapore's Compulsory Education Act, demonstrate that phased legislation can drive meaningful change by allowing adequate preparation time for education and capability building.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I have seven key elements to be included.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: First, review and enhance the effectiveness and outreach of the existing programmes, such as the Open Door Programme, the Place and Train Programme and the Job Placement and Support Scheme.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two, extend the Enabling Mark concept from beyond employers to service providers, such as job placement agencies and coaches, whether they are Government-supported or not, to ensure better support and quality assurance for employers and PwDs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Third, enlarge and professionalise the pool of job and life coaches.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Fifth, develop a joint national service between the Ministry of Manpower and SG Enable under the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF), modeled on the Job Accommodation Network (JAN) in the United States, to guide employers in implementing reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: JAN's online database of best practices, live chat support and tailored solutions is a model that Singapore can learn from and adapt.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In fact, Singapore can have our own version of JAN, which should also the education and guiding employees with disabilities so that they can be stronger in self-advocacy, showing also sensitivity to their employers' business needs, understanding what is reasonable on their part and also taking proactive steps that they, like anyone else, can take to support themselves in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, let us help PwDs, employees with disabilities themselves, at the workplace to self-advocate.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And lastly, to ensure measurement and accountability through annual progress reports on readiness and inclusion metrics, that is, for developing the roadmap for legislation to include reasonable accommodations by 2030.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am not asking for targets or quotas.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I am asking for whatever is done, we need to scale it.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Agencies like the National Library Board, VITAL, GovTech, the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Board, the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF), the Ministry of Health (MOH) Holdings, Singapore General Hospital (SGH) and several more, they have already seriously embarked on inclusive hiring and doing quite well, giving jobs in blue-, white- and new-collar spaces.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, scaling these efforts will set the tone for private sector adoption and aspire a community of practice.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, the public sector should take leadership in this.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: So, Sir, in conclusion, the Workplace Fairness Bill is a necessary step forward in protecting workers against discrimination.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: To make a real difference for PwDs, reasonable accommodations must, eventually, be legislated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I urge the Government, PwDs and their advocates and employers and families as well, to each take our place and create and support an inclusive Singapore workforce.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Bill that this House is debating today is much-needed and a long-overdue one, if we pride ourselves on being an open and inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The passage of a Workplace Fairness Bill in Singapore is not just a legislative necessity.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is a moral imperative that addresses the long-standing issue of workplace discrimination that has affected many workers across various sectors.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For too long, employees have faced barriers based on age, race and other personal characteristics without adequate legal protections, which not only undermine their dignity but also hampers our nation's commitment to meritocracy and equality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In WP's 2020 manifesto, we called for the institution of anti-discrimination legislation on the basis of gender, race and age.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Importantly, the manifesto also notes how the Government's strategy of issuing advisories and guidelines does not penalise employers sufficiently for adopting discriminatory practices.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The contents of this Bill largely reflect the Government's approach towards the issue of fair employment practices and the focus on harmonious workplace relations in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I will be touching on a few areas in which I believe there could be areas of improvement to consider, especially as we look to introduce a second Bill on this matter later in 2025.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first broad point I wish to highlight is the issue of exclusions in this Workplace Fairness Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Granted, workplace fairness and the issue of discrimination are complex ones and the Government may want to take an incremental and cautious approach towards legislation in this area.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, if we are deliberately looking at discrimination in the narrow sense through careful scoping of the Bill, how confident are we in saying that this new legislation will be effective in addressing the concerns and discriminatory barriers of minorities?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: How can we confidently say that workplace discrimination of any form should not be tolerated, but yet, some forms of discrimination are illegal while others are not?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There are, however, several other classes of people who may face discrimination, but yet will not be covered by this Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The first is on physical medical conditions, as I note that mental health conditions are a protected characteristic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I have met residents who have been through a period of medical illness, which has resulted in them being unable to work for an extended period of time, causing them to rack up a significant medical bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: What could be more distressing, however, is that they may face a major hurdle as employers may view their medical history as a liability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For instance, a resident of mine is on follow-up with a cardiologist for a cardiac condition.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, he was specifically certified by the doctor that from a cardiac perspective, he was fit-to-work based on the nature of his job scope.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, despite this, he believes that he was being terminated more than once by different employers because of his condition and especially, when one of them only required him to perform guest services-related duties in an indoor location.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The draft Health Information Bill, which was opened for public consultation in 2023, prohibits the use of National Electronic Health Record data for non-patient purposes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Being an open and inclusive country, Singapore must also grant second chances to those who are keen on joining the workforce after a stint in prison.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Although such members of our society are willing and motivated to contribute productively, a CNA article highlights that many of them face discrimination when job-hunting despite being qualified for the role.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, it is only right that those with a past criminal record are also protected against workplace discrimination under this new law.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In certain instances, it could be arguable that restrictions are put in place, given the risks involved.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, under section 26 of the Child Care Centres Regulations, staff who have been convicted of offences, such as child abuse and neglect, are not allowed to be hired as staff of a childcare centre.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the financial industry, in response to my PQ in August 2024, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong shared that the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) does not restrict the hiring of ex-offenders in the financial industry in all instances.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Rather, it issues prohibition orders to specific individuals who have committed serious offences or misconduct in the financial industry and an ex-offender who has not been issued any prohibition order or an individual whose prohibition order has expired may be employed by a financial institution, if he or she has been assessed to be fit and proper for the role.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Yet, the assessment of whether a person is fit and proper can be a subjective one and at present, MAS does not track the number of ex-offenders hired by financial institutions or require financial institutions to inform MAS of the rejection of candidates.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would certainly open more doors for them to start afresh and rebuild their lives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Beyond the issue of protected characteristics, one of the other glaring omissions in the Bill is that on indirect discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Aside from being difficult to detect, workplace discrimination comes in all shapes and forms.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this Bill covers direct discrimination, which refers to an instance where someone is treated less favourably than someone else in a comparable situation on the basis of a protected characteristic, my Sengkang colleague He Ting Ru observed that the proposed Bill does not cover discrimination by association, which is when someone is treated less favourably as they are acquainted with someone who possesses a protected characteristic.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Furthermore, discrimination by perception, which is when someone is treated unfairly as they are falsely believed to possess a protected characteristic, is also beyond the remit of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Examples of indirect discrimination may include working hours that unnecessarily disadvantage employees with children, or perhaps an attire policy that unreasonably discriminates against employees from a particular racial or religious group.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: According to a Parliamentary reply by Manpower Minister Tan See Leng, he noted that including indirect discrimination as part of the Bill would "impose very wide legal obligations on employers", which results in "uncertainty for both employees and employers alike".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instances of indirect discrimination could be reported to TAFEP instead.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, having two separate frameworks, one enshrined in law and the other based on guidelines for handling discrimination, may also cause confusion to both employers and employees alike.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Instead of omitting it from the Bill entirely, I suggest that as an intermediary step, guidance be provided to educate employers and their staff on indirect discrimination, its seriousness and the importance of addressing it appropriately.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: If we look at UK case law, it establishes a precedent regarding what constitutes indirect discrimination and how such cases are to be handled.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: According to a UK Supreme Court ruling, employees need not prove why a Provision, Criteria or Practice (PCP) disadvantages people of a particular group in order to show indirect discrimination but instead requires a causal link between the PCP and the particular disadvantage suffered by the group and the individual.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: At the same time, it is open to an employer to show that their PCP is justified and there will be no finding of unlawful discrimination unless the justification is not made out.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One key instance of indirect discrimination would be the denial of reasonable accommodation, which would be useful for certain workers, such as those with disabilities and older workers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Clause 15 of the Bill refers to someone with a disability as an individual who has any one or more of the following, namely autism, any intellectual disability, any physical disability and/or any sensory disability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: PwDs face an uphill climb when navigating through the various hurdles in society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Worryingly, there was also a decrease in the percentage of respondents who expressed positive attitudes toward PwDs in the workplace compared to the last survey in 2019.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is imperative that Singaporeans ought to cultivate a society where our PwDs could feel included.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While mindset shifts are certainly crucial, we also ought to strengthen our legislative tools to create a barrier-free society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Bill's coverage of PwDs under clause 8 would certainly offer greater protection for PwDs against discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, one of the barriers that PwDs experience when seeking gainful employment is the lack of reasonable accommodations in their workplaces.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: According to the CRPD, reasonable accommodations are "necessary and appropriate adjustments" to ensure that in the workplace, PwDs would be able to function "on an equal basis with others on all human rights and fundamental freedoms".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Examples of reasonable accommodation include ensuring step-free access to workplaces for employees with mobility issues and work-from-home arrangements for workers with sensory impairments.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: There have been governmental programmes to encourage business to implement reasonable accommodations for PwDs, such as SG Enable's Job Redesign Grant.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As pointed out in a report by the Disabled People's Association, in their 2022 Concluding Observations to Singapore, the UNCRPD noted on more than one occasion within their recommendations to the Singapore Government on the need to prohibit the denial of reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, it is "concerned about the lack of recognition of denial of reasonable accommodation as a form of discrimination on the basis of disability" in Singapore and recommends that Singapore "adopt legal provisions and create practice to recognise denial of reasonable accommodation as a form of discrimination in all areas of life and include an express definition of reasonable accommodation consistent with Article 2 of the Convention".

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To ensure its effective implementation, the Tripartite Advisory for Reasonable Accommodations could function as a source of guidance for employers and employees alike.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Besides PwDs, other workers, such as those with caregiving duties, parents and older workers, would also benefit from reasonable accommodations in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The second point I am concerned about is the requirement that TAFEP serve as the first port of call outside the firm for workers who experience discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While this is a point to be covered under the second Workplace Fairness Bill, I hope that the Government can give this point due consideration, before it is being raised for First Reading.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Now that we have made the all-important step to introduce legislation to combat discrimination, I am concerned that having TAFEP and TADM as the first port of call could mean that, in practice, we are back at square one and there may not be much of a difference to the current means to deal with discrimination via the TAFEP guidelines.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While the articulated aim by the Government is to preserve workplace harmony, in the case of a termination of employment, we can be clear that there is no intention by the employer to be in a continuing work relationship with the employee, much less a harmonious one and it is more likely going to be an acrimonious rather than harmonious relationship after the termination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Relying on mediation could place employees at a disadvantage, as they may lack the resources, such as time, energy, money and support to effectively challenge powerful and well-resourced employers.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Mediation can often also favour the more dominant party, leading to outcomes that do not adequately address the grievances of those who experience discrimination and wrongful termination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This brings me to the third broad point I wish to highlight in that the ease at which employees can be terminated.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To successfully claim that a dismissal with notice is wrongful, where no reason is given for the dismissal, an employee must substantiate a wrongful reason for the dismissal, for example, discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The point about circumstantial evidence is thus an important one, given the colossal task faced by employees in proving discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is not easy to detect workplace discrimination as employers would attempt to hide it.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, employers would not indicate in black and white that an employee is being terminated due to their age.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But rather, the said employee would perhaps hear it via word-of-mouth from a fellow colleague.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In fact, they might even hear it directly from the line managers in passing, but have no concrete recording or evidence of it, allowing him or her to subsequently deny having said such a thing at all.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, the employee would most likely have at best indirect or circumstantial evidence of any wrongdoing by the employer in such cases.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The establishment of a framework for the handling of indirect evidence would be helpful for workers who might be afraid of seeking redress as they feel that they lack substantial evidence.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For instance, in US case law, the Mcdonnell Douglas burden-shifting framework places the burden of proof on employers to argue that there is a justification for their employment decision, after the employee has ascertained that they are rejected from a role despite being qualified for the job.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: A key tenet of this Bill is also to ensure that Singaporeans and PRs are fairly considered for employment.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is reflected in the implementation of the FCF under clause 26 of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, employers may also pre-select a candidate and go through the motions of interviewing applicants from the MyCareersFuture portal without considering them fairly.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, how is the Government monitoring such employers and how would such employers be penalised?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Would the Government also consider implementing a mechanism that monitors the outcomes of job postings uploaded to MyCareersFuture?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On a related note, one crucial development in the HR industry is the proliferation of AI in the hiring process.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For instance, an Applicant Tracking Software (ATS) could be used to filter out curriculum vitaes based on the employer's needs, while an AI-powered video-interviewing software could analyse the candidate's speech and behaviour.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, AI could also perpetuate discrimination if the algorithm or data is biased.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Minister also highlighted the Model AI Governance Framework for Generative AI, which encourages AI developers to adopt data quality control measures and to disclose information regarding the AI model's make-up.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, it is crucial to unpack the "black box" that is AI to ensure that it is not a tool deployed by employers to enable discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Candidates must also be informed when AI is being used during the hiring process.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Aside from mitigating the risk of discrimination arising from the usage of AI systems, this would also help to assuage public scepticism towards AI's usage in recruitment due to its perceived unfairness compared to a human recruiter.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On that note, while mindset changes amongst employers and employees are a key ingredient towards building a fairer workplace, the legislation that we pass in this House sends a signal about where our priorities lie and charts a direction in which society heads towards.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As cliché as it may sound, if we wish to build a society that is "based on justice and equality" that ensures "happiness, prosperity, and progress for our nation", then we should take greater strides in ensuring that within every facet of society, everyone will have the opportunity to thrive and flourish.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It strikes a necessary balance between an employee's right to redress and an employer's need to manage operations effectively.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my speech, I will raise the following three points: one, concerns about a litigious work environment are addressed through a mediation-first approach to foster trust and reduce disputes; two, resource limitation challenges that smaller enterprises may face in implementing the Bill, the unintended consequences of exemption and initiatives, such as HR-as-a-service to support SMEs; and three, the need to equip HR professionals, managers, employees and jobseekers with training and resources for consistent understanding and fair application of the law while proactively aligning employee expectations with employer capabilities to foster a harmonious and inclusive workplace.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Regarding my first point, there are concerns that additional legislation might lead to increased litigations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In some cases, while addressing unfair treatment, this has led to overcorrection by employers, resulting in rigid procedures rather than fostering trust.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is also the fear of lawsuits, which sometimes stifled open communication.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The proposed Bill targets familiar and common forms of discrimination.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By maintaining clear definitions and focusing on prevalent issues, we reduce the likelihood of disputes requiring legal interventions while ensuring broad coverage.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, the UK's Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service resolves most disputes before they reach tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Here, employees will be encouraged to seek internal resolutions first.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If that fails, mediation through TAFEP or TADM will follow.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Only as a last resort, will cases proceed to the Employment Claims Tribunals.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This tiered approach prioritises workplace harmony and encourages efficient and equitable resolutions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Regarding my second point on the potential burden on employers, particularly smaller businesses.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In the UK, the proposed Employment Rights Bill is projected to raise business costs by billions annually.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Similarly, Canada's Employment Equity Act demands extensive reporting and complex policies, while Australia's Fair Work Act has driven many employers to seek costly legal advice to avoid compliance errors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore's economy depends on an ecosystem of multinational corporations, SMEs and startups.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Smaller enterprises, in particular, are concerned about the administrative costs of compliance, such as hiring consultants, lawyers or additional staff.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An unintended consequence could be that employees may avoid smaller companies, perceiving them as offering weaker workplace protections.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This could worsen the existing talent attraction and retention challenges faced by SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To address this, there is an urgent need to support smaller companies in understanding and implementing the Bill effectively.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a measure would enable forward-thinking SMEs to enhance their employer branding and position themselves as employers of choice.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a service could be facilitated by the IHRP, which is well-positioned to pool HR expertise and deliver scalable solutions for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Workplace Fairness Bill sets minimum standards, a welcome step in signalling to errant employers that workplace fairness is non-negotiable.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At the same time, we must also recognise and reward progressive HR practices.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The SHRI's annual Singapore HR Awards is one such initiative, but there is potential to enhance and expand these efforts.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Regarding my third point, good legislation sets standards, but it is ultimately HR professionals, supervisors and team leaders who translates standards into fair outcomes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must ensure they are equipped to interpret and apply the law confidently and consistently.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore can do better by offering robust support.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through partnerships with SNEF, NTUC and TAFEP, the Government will prepare materials, conduct outreach and provide practical tools to train HR professionals, hiring managers and supervisors.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These resources will help them identify discrimination, handle grievances effectively and communicate decisions.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With proper training, managers can apply the rules confidently, reducing the likelihood of disputes and fostering a culture of fairness.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, fostering workplace harmony requires a concerted effort from both employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While much training focuses on employers, we must also empower employees and jobseekers.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The TADM currently provides advisory services to manage employment or payment-related disputes, but more proactive measures are needed.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would also promote greater alignment between employee expectations and employers' resource capacities.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By posing these questions today, we acknowledge that implementing this Bill will be a journey.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must stay vigilant, ensuring stakeholders have the resources they need and remain open to improvements.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While these figures highlight improvement, discrimination remains a concern for many Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond these statistics are deeply personal stories of exclusion and unfair treatment, underscoring the importance of continued action, and I thank Minister Tan for acknowledging that.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, I recall moments from my career, both in Singapore and abroad, where I faced discrimination as a minority.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a young engineer in Singapore, I was once told, "You are quite smart, for a Malay".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I also felt excluded when colleagues held meetings entirely in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Overseas, when I was mistaken for a Latino American, I encountered overt racial prejudice.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These experiences, shared by many, reminds us that discrimination persist in both overt and subtle forms.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Tackling these issues requires sustained efforts to create a fairer, more inclusive society, where opportunities are accessible to all, regardless of race, religion or other attributes.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Together, these measures reflect Singapore's commitment to fostering workplaces where everyone can thrive.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I seek clarification on three areas: firstly, the definition of character of protected characteristics; secondly, the application of the Bill; and thirdly, the grievance resolution process and its effectiveness.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While the inclusion of these protected characteristics is a great step forward, the legislation remains punitive in nature.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Legislation is an important step, but how do we shift from punishing discrimination to actively fostering the employment of seniors, PwDs and caregivers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How can the Workplace Fairness Legislation work in tandem with the tripartite guidelines on fair employment practices, to tackle workplace discrimination holistically?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For many seniors seeking employment, discrimination remains painfully real.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some are denied even an interview once their age is revealed.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This reflects entrenched biasness that legislation alone cannot address.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Beyond punitive measures, how will we challenge and change such ingrained attitudes to create an inclusive mindset among employers?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Jobseekers must understand their rights and avoid providing sensitive information like age, race, religion or marital status on their CVs, a practice once very common.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Schools, career services and organisations like e2i and Workforce Singapore should embed this knowledge in career preparation efforts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, some employers still request sensitive personal details during the application process.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Clearer guidelines must discourage such practices to ensure equal opportunities for all candidates, and by addressing these systemic issues alongside the legislative framework, we can move closer to workplace culture rooted in fairness and inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Can TGFEP recommend that employers provide upfront clarity on why a characteristic is necessary, such as specifying that language proficiency, is required for customer interaction in specific markets?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, if the Chinese language ability is required, the advert could read "Chinese-speaking preferred as employee is required to address customers from the Chinese market".

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Having such details would definitely help remove the perceived discrimination.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Reasonable accommodation refers to modification or adjustments to enable employees with disabilities to perform essential job functions and enjoy equal employment benefits.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For instance, adapting a workspace for an employee with a physical disability is relatively straight-forward.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, cases like accommodating someone with anxiety disorder requesting a completely quiet workplace, with less people in an office and set away from others can pose significant practical and financial challenges.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, I understand why the Bill may have avoided explicitly addressing reasonable accommodation – ambiguities in its interpretation could lead to disputes, increasing the risk of a litigious culture where formal adjudication becomes the default mechanism for resolving uncertainties.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, under the Americans with Disabilities Act in the US, which mandates employers to provide reasonable accommodation, numerous cases have ended in formal adjudication due to disagreements over what constitutes "reasonable." However, we cannot simply discard the principle of reasonable accommodation because of its complexities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The critical question is: how can we address genuine cases of reasonable accommodation effectively under WFL and TGFEP?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Recommendation 13 of the TGFEP suggests that TAFEP issues advisories and facilitates dialogues between employees and employers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While this is promising, it remains too ambiguous to drive meaningful change.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To advance inclusivity, we must strengthen our approach.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: WFL or TGFEP should mandate, or at least, strongly encourage, organisations to establish clear processes for reasonable accommodation requests.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Linking this effort with the work of the taskforce on Inclusive Employment Practices under the Enabling Masterplan 2030 can provide financial support and resources, reducing employer burden and fostering workplace inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Burden on employers and encourage the hiring of persons with disabilities, making workplace inclusivity a tangible reality.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My second clarification links to the application of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What percentage of our workforce is not covered under this Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While I understand the phased approach, when will WFL apply to smaller organisations?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the meantime, how will we prepare these companies with more robust HR practices?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: My third clarification is on the process of resolving grievances.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How does the legislation safeguard the identity of the complainants and protect them from retaliation?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How will the Ministry support firms in developing effective processes to meet WFL requirements?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Could this lead to a more litigious culture, particularly around subjective areas, like performance appraisals and promotions?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: What volume of cases does the Ministry anticipate under this framework and what proportion might escalate to formal adjudication?

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Success hinges on the organisations' ability to resolve issues internally and TAFEP's capacity to mediate.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workplace discrimination among workers in Singapore was also at 8%, which is significantly lower than the European Union average of 11%.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Despite these improvements, discrimination remains real, emphasising the need for continued efforts to address this issue.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a minority, I have also faced discrimination like many minority communities in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And I would like to thank Minister Tan for highlighting that, although the number is not as high as before, there are still cases of racial and religious discrimination.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In one of my previous jobs in Singapore, I was once told, "You're quite smart... for a Malay," and felt marginalised when colleagues held meetings entirely in Mandarin.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Unfortunately, I also had the chance to compare the discrimination faced in other countries when I faced more overt racial discrimination such as being called derogatory names due to the colour of my skin.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: These experiences reflect how discrimination can manifest both subtly and overtly, and this is a common experience of many from minority groups.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Workplace Fairness Bill to protect against discrimination, including those based on race, language and language, is a significant step forward.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Discrimination is a complex issue that requires ongoing efforts.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Workplace Fairness legislation itself is not a panacea, but rather a measured additional protection for our workers.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Although the law will play its role will play a part, individuals can also protect themselves from discrimination through personal resilience—by enhancing their skills and achieving excellence in their respective fields to eliminate any doubts about their capabilities.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Individuals can strive to be the best candidate for their job, leaving no room for prejudice.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, I would like to suggest that the Workplace Fairness Bill require employers to explain the necessity of certain characteristics, such as language proficiency.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For example, if language proficiency is required to deal with customers from the China market, the job advertisement could state that, "The ability to speak Chinese is encouraged in order to deal with customers from the China market." This would help remove any perceived discrimination.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While workplace fairness has certainly improved, creating a more just society with equal opportunities requires an ongoing effort.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Together, through legislation and individual action, we can build a more inclusive and equitable workplace for all. : Mr Speaker, notwithstanding the clarification sought, I stand firmly in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Sharael Taha (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It represents a pivotal step towards a fairer workplace and a more inclusive society.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Discrimination, in all its forms, must be eradicated if we are to build a truly inclusive community.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As the saying goes, "the true measure of any society can be found in how it treats its most vulnerable members".

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill reflects that principle, representing a step forward in the right direction and I commend the Government for reaffirming our pledge to fairness and dignity.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Among them, disability has been designated as one protected characteristic, bringing much-needed attention to a vulnerable minority.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: My speech will focus on what this legislation means for those with disabilities in the employment landscape.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Under section 17 of the Bill, it is discrimination for an employer to make an employment decision that adversely affects an individual if at least one of the grounds for the decision includes the individual's protected characteristic.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This means that direct discrimination is expressly prohibited.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot allow fair employment opportunities to be denied on the basis of one's disability.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Indirect discrimination occurs when a seemingly neutral policy disproportionately puts persons with a particular protected characteristic at a disadvantage, even if the adverse outcome is unintended.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For example, sharing key information solely through verbal communication would exclude employees who are deaf or hard of hearing and pose challenges for autistic individuals who need direct and explicit messaging.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: An employer might believe they are being fair by giving instructions to all employees in the same way.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: They may think there is no discriminatory practice.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: But this approach disadvantages those of us who genuinely require tailored adjustments to thrive.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: When accessibility is disregarded, opportunities at the workplace gradually narrow.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The result is an adverse employment outcome that unjustly penalises someone for circumstances beyond their control.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It may be subtle and less obvious, but it is a real issue that needs to be tackled.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Policies or common practices are rarely designed with sufficient thought for including minorities or the disadvantaged.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This makes indirect discrimination more pervasive and harder to address, especially when biases are unconscious.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Without sufficient intervention, it leaves disadvantaged minorities even more vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In the absence of legislation, those who believe they have suffered from indirect discrimination have little recourse besides seeking help from TAFEP.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Employers and employees in Singapore who wish to understand the principles of fair employment practices can refer to TAFEP's TGFEP.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The guidelines outline the dos and do nots for ensuring fairness across all stages of employment.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: However, the current recommendations and examples that accompany them deal only with direct discrimination.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Since protections against direct discrimination will now be elevated through legislation, the issue of indirect discrimination remains insufficiently addressed in existing guidelines.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Given this, can MOM consider, in collaboration with the tripartite partners, updating and improving the guidelines to incorporate explicit messaging that indirect discrimination is not to be tolerated?

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These guidelines should include clear examples of indirect discrimination.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: By helping employers and employees better understand the concept, the TGFEP can serve as a valuable tool for providing practical guidance for employers and employees to navigate such situations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This may be especially helpful for employers with fewer than 25 employees who are currently not in the scope of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Most who experienced discrimination at work often do not report to official channels.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, they believed that their concerns will not be taken seriously, or worse, that they will face negative consequences.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Under section 28 of the Bill, "prohibition against retaliation", only prohibits retaliation for anything done under or by reference to the proposed Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is unclear if these protections extend to those who seek help from TAFEP or MOM for indirect discrimination.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is crucial that those who suffer from discrimination feel safe and empowered to report such unfortunate instances.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Given this, can the Government clarify, how employees who seek help in cases of indirect discrimination will be protected against retaliation since this falls, technically, outside of the Bill's coverage.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Addressing this clearly will encourage more employees to come forward without fear of reprisal, ensuring they report their concerns and finally receive the support they need.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While the Government has chosen not to include protections for indirect discrimination in the Bill at this juncture, such legislation is not new.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: There are other jurisdictions that have legally defined indirect discrimination to protect vulnerable persons in all settings beyond just the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, the UK has its Equality Act.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Australia makes this definition in its Disability Discrimination Act as well as in the respective discrimination Acts for age and sex.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly in Hong Kong, the Ordinances for each protected attribute of disability, sex, family status and race, all explicitly provide for protections against indirect discrimination.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The passing of the Workplace Fairness Act is an important step in helping our workplace mature, paving the way for deeper commitments to fairness and inclusivity in the future.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
