text: In parallel, I urge the Government to examine how other jurisdictions have defined and implemented such protections against indirect discrimination and adapt these learnings to strengthen our local approach in future amendments to our WFL.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: One such form is the denial of reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is recognised in some jurisdictions as a discriminatory practice.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Taking reference from SG Enable and the UNCRPD, reasonable accommodations are necessary and appropriate modifications and adjustments.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: They are adjustments that do not impose a disproportionate or undue burden and puts persons with disabilities on equal footing with the rest of society.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Many of us rarely consider the accommodations we rely on daily, like having a table to write on or a chair to sit on, because they are so integrated into our lives.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Just as having a table or a computer is a basic necessity for work, PwDs also need accommodations – only that they are tailored to their specific needs to carry out their tasks effectively.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: For example, a wheelchair user may require a height-adjustable desk at work.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: An autistic employee might benefit from a relaxed dress code to reduce sensory discomfort or require clear, direct instructions to enable productive work delivery.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: PwDs merely want to be treated equitably, not with sympathy or pity.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In place of legislation, I understand that the tripartite partners plan to release an advisory on the provision of reasonable accommodations for persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is expected to work in concert with the WFL.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We all know an advisory is not law, but if harnessed effectively, it could still lay important groundwork.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: If we want employers to embrace and buy into the idea of reasonable accommodation, we must first demonstrate its necessity, share best practices and debunk the myths.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Taking this stepwise approach may be a prudent way to build consensus and readiness, before moving towards strengthening our law in the near future.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: To ensure the advisory is effective, I would like to offer a few suggestions.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: First, the advisory needs to emphasise that reasonable accommodations are a necessity, not a good-to-have.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It needs to address common misconceptions and clearly show that the outcome is a net positive to the employer and the employee.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In the context of workplaces, reasonable accommodations are indispensable adjustments made to enable persons with disabilities to perform their job duties.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The goal of reasonable accommodations is not to give anyone an unfair advantage.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It allows persons with disabilities to enjoy equal opportunities in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: According to the US Job Accommodation Network, 85% of employers reported a direct benefit of retaining a valuable employee as a result of having made an accommodation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Other widely mentioned benefits include increased employee productivity and company morale.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These points show that when employees are given the right tools and environment, they are happier and well positioned to become valuable contributors that stay for the long term.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Second, the advisory should draw attention to the financial support available to allay any costs concerns.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Reasonable accommodations are not meant to be overwhelming or create excessive strain on any organisation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Some employers may worry that providing accommodations would come at a heavy cost.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The US Job Accommodation Network found that 56% of workplace accommodations for persons with disabilities came at no cost to employers – free of charge.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Another 37% experienced a one-off cost with a median of US$300 or roughly S$410.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Closer to home, Singapore offers grants specifically designed to support employers in creating workplace accommodations for persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The grant, administered by SG Enable, can be used to defray the cost for the purchase of equipment, workplace modifications, redesigning of job scopes or processes and consultancy services.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: We need to do more to encourage higher uptake of available support.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that the tripartite partners can play a crucial role in raising awareness of such schemes.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Third, the advisory needs to outline how the process of providing reasonable accommodations should be managed.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Requesting for accommodations is not a one-sided demand.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Instead, it should be a collaborative process that addresses concerns of both employees and employers.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This can be clarified by providing specific examples of reasonable accommodations and what falls outside the scope of reasonableness.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This balanced approach ensures that such workplace accommodations are validated and implemented in a practical and fair manner.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Our very debate today is one such example.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Direct discrimination was once only addressed in the TGFEP.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Now, protections against direct discrimination are enshrined in law.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Another example is the recently introduced Tripartite Guidelines on Flexible Work Arrangement Requests, which replaced the earlier tripartite advisory on FWAs.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The same approach can be applied to reasonable accommodations in the future.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While an advisory can serve to provide a starting point, there is a real risk it may not be taken seriously or is seen as optional.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, it is crucial that the transition into enforceable guidelines is prompt and deliberate.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As employers adapt to new practices under the advisory, the Government can study how to legislate reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: On the surface, defining what is "reasonable" might sound tricky, but it is not an abstract concept.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Just like for indirect discrimination, other jurisdictions provide for reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This is scoped not to only provide coverage for PwDs, but to cover all other prohibited grounds of discrimination, which means protected characteristics in our context.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It also states that, "the Governor in Council may make regulations prescribing standards for assessing undue hardship".

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In determining whether a hardship is unjustifiable, the Disability Discrimination Act adopts a multifactorial approach by taking into account all relevant circumstances of the particular case.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: These legal frameworks, while not identical, all uphold a holistic and thoughtfully applied principle of reasonableness, which safeguards the vulnerable while ensuring a judicious process.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: By studying how other jurisdictions have embedded their laws into practice, we can refine our approach and adapt these lessons to Singapore's unique context.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The Disability Trends report released by MSF last month revealed that public attitudes towards persons with disabilities were largely positive.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: While the reasons for this are not stated by MSF, more work needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: NCSS' survey also revealed one interesting finding, which I will quote: "respondents who had contact with persons with disabilities at least twice in the past year reported higher proportions of positive public attitudes across the four disability types, compared to those who had no contact with persons with disabilities at all".

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: This highlights the need to consistently raise awareness and promote meaningful interactions in the community.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: The more we live, play or work with PwDs, the more understanding and accepting we become.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: I agree with Minister Tan See Leng – there is no silver bullet to eradicate discrimination.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Legislation alone cannot be a panacea that solves for fair and nurturing workplaces.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: As we debate the finer points today, we must not lose sight of the bigger picture.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: In 2013, Singapore ratified the UNCRPD and we have done a lot since.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Today marks a meaningful step in our ongoing effort to address the remaining gaps in our laws.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: But the passing of this Bill will not be of material concern for employers who are already inclusive, nor will it automatically transform every organisation into an equitable employer.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It simply sets the minimum standards for fair employment practices.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is my hope that more employers take fairness beyond just a legal obligation.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: It is an opportunity to embrace the benefits of workplace diversity and above all, to do what is right.

speaker: Mr Ong Hua Han (Nominated Member)
text: Let us continue striving for a Singapore where every individual is valued and where our workplaces reflect the best of our shared values.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the course of us going about our daily lives, we have heard and bore witness to acts or words of discrimination.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just this weekend, during my block visit in Punggol, one resident shared with me his challenges in finding a job when he was retrenched.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He is 62, and during a job interview, the interviewer commented that he was the same age as her father.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The interview, charming as it was, did not turn out well for my resident, as there was a low-humming preconception that he was too "senior" for the position, both in age and in experience.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is a form of discrimination and one that this Bill serves to address.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our union leaders have told us that discrimination against women in the workplace circle around pregnancy, caregiving and gender role stereotypes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Hence, the Labour Movement welcomes the introduction of the Workplace Fairness Legislation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This marks a significant milestone for Singapore and the Labour Movement towards levelling the playing field for women and caregivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This journey has been a long and deliberate one towards this Bill and one that has been championed by many generations of female union leaders.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As early as 2007, then NTUC Assistant Secretary-General Mdm Halimah Yacob called on the MOM to address discrimination against pregnant employees beyond dismissal, highlighting the need for proper HR practices and fair access to opportunities.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In 2018, our President Thanaletchimi, then Nominated Member of Parliament, pushed for a more targeted approach to enhance the adoption of tripartite standards, recognising their crucial role in grievance handling and FWAs.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I, more recently in 2022 and 2024, advocated for fair employment practices for caregivers on FWAs and had asked for more support for companies to implement progressive performance appraisals.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have made great strides in making the workplace fairer for females and caregivers.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, Mr Speaker, statistically low as they seem, behind these statistics are real people with real challenges and it is important that this Bill forms part of the larger ecosystem of protection.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Redressing discrimination is not new to the Labour Movement.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Kelly, not her real name, is a resident of mine and an NTUC union member.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Just before Kelly started on a new full-time job, she found out that she was pregnant and decided to inform her future employer.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: She was presented then with two options, either work part-time or work full-time but only for two months.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To my team, this was an attempt by her future employer to avoid providing maternity benefits, though ironically, the employer seemed unaware that maternity benefits apply to part-time employees as well.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Understandably, Kelly was no longer keen to join the company.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As a union member, we put Kelly in touch with TADM@NTUC and they managed to negotiate with the company to cancel her employment agreement without penalties.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And with the help of the Women and Family Unit, Kelly subsequently found work near Punggol where she stays and embarked on a fruitful career as an educarer.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The example given would highlight the importance of union membership and representation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I seek clarification on the Ministry's investigation and enforcement measures should employers run afoul of the TGFEP.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Indeed, for this legislation to truly succeed, we must ensure its effective implementation.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A 2022 survey by Women and Family Unit and the PAP Women's Wing highlighted some concerns.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Women perceive that they are disproportionately facing workplace discrimination and highlighted the prevalence of a lack of company know-how and policy against such workforce discrimination and harassment, particularly among companies that do not enjoy the abundance of resources and manpower.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This possibly suggests that women are less likely to report gender discrimination.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In addition, the fear of retaliation and the lack of clear reporting procedures were main reasons that discouraged the reporting of workplace gender discrimination.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: While companies we spoke with welcomed this legislation and shared that this provides a fair level playing field amongst companies with the same rules at play, many were worried about implementing this effectively.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some quoted the lack of understanding when it comes to the finer details of employment laws and for others, the lack of resources when coming out with progressive HR policies and practices.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: One recent case that my team at the NTUC USME, the department that works with SMEs and SME workers came across, was an aggrieved female worker who reported on an unfair clause in her employment contract.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is a discriminating practice and when we spoke with the business owner about the clause, he shared that he was unaware that it was there in the first place and was sincerely aghast about the matter.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: He and his team are now part of the Labour Movement and are working with the NTUC on coming up with better worker outcomes.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To promote better fairer workplaces, the NTUC together with our tripartite partners, have provided advice, templates, playbooks and training for our SME workers and business owners.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: By the way, breastfeeding in the workplace is a protected characteristic of "pregnancy" under the proposed Bill.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: An interim measure could also be to recognise SMEs who have implemented WFL practices in their workplaces voluntarily.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This will allow all companies to be on a level playing field and to uplift the image of SMEs to be equally progressive employers alongside all Singaporean companies.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Like fleas confined in a jar, the WFL cannot be the jar that conditions and limits us to how high we can jump.

speaker: Ms Yeo Wan Ling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Workplace fairness must become a societal norm because every worker matters.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: My speech today will touch on the importance of protecting workers with mental health conditions and to ensure that workers working in small businesses do not fall through the cracks during the transition period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to a June 2024 survey by Telus Health, almost half of the 1,000 workers surveyed in Singapore reported feeling exhausted after a day's work.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The company which commissioned the survey said that these findings point to the growing risk of burnout among workers and highlighted a need for greater mental health support.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: According to a 2022 study by The Instant Group, Singapore was found to be the most overworked country in the Asia Pacific region.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Straits Times also reported recently in November 2024, that stress bragging, that is bragging of overworked, was becoming more prevalent at the workplace, with negative consequences on workplace culture and relationships.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Despite this, unfortunately, many workers remain afraid to speak up or seek help for their mental health issues, because of the perceived negative attitudes and reactions from others.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Some also worry that they will be discriminated against during employment decisions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In NTUC's own #EveryWorkerMatters Conversations, young workers shared with us that, while they felt mental health support was important, only about a quarter of them felt that there have been improvements in the way society and the workplace treat individuals with mental health issues.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: However, I have some questions and some suggestions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: In effect, this would mean that workers with mental health conditions are only protected from discrimination if they see and are treated by a psychiatrist.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: There is a wide array of mental health conditions, with a range of treatment options, depending on how early someone seeks assistance.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Beyond the clinical environment of seeing a psychiatrist, some workers with milder mental health issues would benefit greatly from seeing a therapist or a psychologist.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Could the Government recognise allied healthcare professionals in the mental health space, as part of our push to protect workers from mental health discrimination?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Singapore Psychological Society today already runs a voluntary register of psychologists.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: The Ministry of Health could amend the Allied Health Professions Act to make registration among psychologists and counsellors mandatory, which would then allow us to expand the definition of a mental health condition under the Workplace Fairness Legislation to include diagnosis by these allied health professionals.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I hope that the Government will seriously consider this proposal.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Under clause 20 of the Bill, employers will need to have genuine job requirements in order to consider protected characteristics when making employment decisions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Would there be white list of jobs provided by MOM, where certain protected characteristics, such as mental health conditions, should be considered?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Without any clarity, I worry that some employers will insist on asking their current and prospective workforce in declaring mental health conditions, even when there are no good reasons to do so.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Next, I would like to highlight the importance of ensuring that workers working in small businesses do not fall through the cracks during the transition period.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Today, there exist companies that seemingly operate under a single brand name but in reality, they are made up of multiple smaller business entitles.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: How would MOM ensure that workers working for such companies have their rights protected during the transition period?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: Mental health issues can be a difficult and complex topic and I hope that the Government will consider an expanded definition of a mental health condition under this Bill to safeguard more workers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Radin Mas)
text: I also hope that the MOM will protect workers working in small businesses during the transition period.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, I would like to offer some clarifications and suggestions that will help ensure its true impact.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This refers to subtle biases, like dismissing their expertise or denying them growth opportunities, not the overt remarks like "you are too old for this job." In my Meet-the-People Sessions, seniors like Mr A, in his 50s, shared how their extensive experience is often overlooked in favor of younger, untested ideas.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Mrs B recounted how she is offered fewer training opportunities, leaving her feeling stagnant and unvalued.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These experiences, though often invisible, create significant barriers to equality.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the Bill addresses training opportunities and prohibits age discrimination, the real challenge lies in detection and resolution.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many seniors hesitate to approach HR, fearing they will be labelled as troublemakers.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Small businesses may not even have formal HR departments to mediate such issues.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To resolve this, we need alternative and non-confrontational channels that allow seniors to address concerns without fear of retaliation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These neutral spaces could facilitate honest dialogue, where employers explain challenges and employees share their feelings of exclusion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This will build trust, foster open communication and ensure that seniors' contributions are fully recognised.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a critical step forward, recognising that mental well-being is as important as physical health.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I am especially heartened that the Bill acknowledges mental health as a protected characteristic without requiring mandatory disclosure.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This voluntary approach should persist as disclosure is only required when there is a measurable impact on performance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Otherwise, mandatory disclosure risks reinforcing stigma and deterring individuals from seeking employment or support.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, we must handle mental health cases sensitively.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The requirement for a formal diagnosis in cases of alleged discrimination is necessary to prevent abuse.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, the process should be handled with compassion and respect, ensuring that employees do not feel alienated or judged.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: I propose greater awareness and education for employers to dispel myths and on the benefits of accommodating employees with mental health conditions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many of these individuals are highly capable when provided the right support.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Training programmes can dispel myths about absenteeism and productivity and equip employers with practical solutions like flexible working hours or quiet spaces.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Such measures will ensure mental health is no longer a barrier to success.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Third, Mr Speaker, Sir, the Bill's exemption for religious organisations as outlined in clause 23 acknowledges their unique roles.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: However, we need to clarify the scope of this exemption to avoid confusion.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Many religious organisations run preschools, charities and welfare services that cater to people of all faiths.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To prevent misunderstandings, I urge the Minister to provide greater clarity on the necessity and limits of these exemptions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Clearer communication will help avoid division and ensure that these provisions are fairly and consistently applied, preserving the harmony we value in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Alternatively, we could offer financial incentives and practical guidance to ease the compliance burden for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Grants for workplace upgrades and training programmes would help SMEs adopt fair practices without placing undue strain on them.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Similarly, reasonable accommodations for persons with disabilities should be addressed.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While larger companies can absorb the costs of accessibility, smaller businesses may struggle.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: TAFEP's advisory and financial support will be critical to ensure that SMEs can create accessible and inclusive workplaces.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will it evolve to meet the challenges of an increasingly digital and AI-enabled world?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The 2024 World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs report reveals that the workplace will be shaped by generative AI, digital transformation and the demand for constant upgrading.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To thrive in this new world, we must harness the power of diversity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Diverse perspectives are no longer just a nice-to-have, they are the key to innovation and success.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The team included not just engineers, they also had anthropologists and historians.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This diversity led to groundbreaking solutions, such as adapting ancient bridge designs for a reliable landing system.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As highlighted in Matthew Syed's "Rebel Ideas", this story exemplifies how embracing diverse minds leads to innovative breakthroughs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It shows us that diversity is not just about representation, it is about creating better and more effective solutions.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It tackles the challenges faced by our senior workers, breaks down barriers for those with mental health conditions, provides clarity on religious exemptions and offers SMEs a thoughtful approach to compliance.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is a call to action for all stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: To employers, value experience, embrace inclusivity and create workplaces where everyone has an equal chance to succeed.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: For persons recovering from and coping with mental health issues, meaningful employment can be both helpful and vital.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: If I would look back over the past 20 years or more, many employers have been extremely generous in providing employment opportunities for persons in recovery.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In the more recent years, with efforts to help persons in recovery gain meaningful employment, even more employers have stepped forward.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Employment support specialists have also been engaged to assist both employees in the workplace and also the employers.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Recent studies and reports show – and have been mentioned by the Minister – that mental health issues will be an area of increasing need for intervention and support.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Including this in the proposed Bill is therefore very timely.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The added complexity for mental health conditions is the issue of stigma.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Individuals may not disclose this even within their family and friends and may also choose not to advise their employers of their condition.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Even of more concern, they may not be willing to seek proper help and suffer in silence.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In order for the individual to be included under mental health condition, there will need to be a professional diagnosis.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: However, the outworking of this will require better understanding and awareness of mental health conditions and the benefits of seeking proper professional intervention.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Public education on mental health and wellness needs to continue.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Employers will also need to better understand mental health conditions and how this may impact the employee and their ability to continue in their roles after appropriate treatment – not unlike other medical issues that result in temporary incapacity to work.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: The workplace must therefore see transformation to one where any person with a mental health condition can be accepted and supported without the agony of stigma.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: While discrimination is addressed in the Bill, the broader challenge of stigma will need continuing efforts.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Many employers have also provided employment opportunities for PwDs.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: For some years now, social enterprises and charities have been active employers for persons with disabilities.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We are also seeing increasingly a much wider group of employers providing employment opportunities for PwDs.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Today, PwDs are prepared for suitable jobs from the time they attend schools.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This therefore removes some of the anxiety, but this will also be dependent on there being enough job vacancies once they enter the job market.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: There also needs to be alignment, as mentioned by hon Member Denise Phua earlier, on conditions that fall under disability.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: One condition is, for example, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, or ADHD.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Statistics show that about two thirds of individuals diagnosed with ADHD present with other disorders which could fall under either the protected characteristic of disability or mental health condition.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: But that would leave out some who are specifically diagnosed with ADHD.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Caregivers, too, have been a group requiring more avenues of support.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: In recent years, more support for caregivers has been provided across various fronts.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: While caregivers are more than likely to be family members as defined, there are caregivers who provide care but fall outside this definition.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill needs to be seen as an initial step towards workplace fairness as it covers broad key areas.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some concern has been raised on whether more clarity should be given in addressing issues arising in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We need to strike a reasonable balance between employers and those who fall under the protected characteristics.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Nevertheless, some degree of recourse as provided in this Bill will help minimise discrimination and unfair practices should these arise.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We should see this as a positive first step and therefore as a work in progress.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Many employers are already providing excellent work environments and giving care to employees who fall under protected characteristics.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Some employers, whether by nature of the sector or other factors, may need time to adjust.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: We should enable this so that every employer can ultimately embrace the intent of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Businesses need to do well in order to do good.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time we want responsible employers who take care of their employees.

speaker: Mr Keith Chua (Nominated Member)
text: Employees, too, must remain diligent and responsible and be reasonable in exercising the protection this Bill provides.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: If workplace fairness is the goal, then reasonable accommodation is the bridge to achieving it for PWDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It is the essential foundation that empowers them to access, sustain and thrive in their livelihoods, fostering equal opportunities not just in employment but also in career growth and development.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Without this bridge, the promise of workplace fairness becomes a hollow ideal.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: In May 2024, MOM shared that the Tripartite Advisory on Reasonable Accommodation would be introduced alongside WFL.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This advisory holds great significance for those in the PwD community, who are keenly awaiting its guidance.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This will serve as a critical framework for fostering inclusive workplaces.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, its importance also highlights why reasonable accommodation cannot remain separate from the discussion on workplace fairness.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Consider this: if a PwD is deemed unsuitable for a role, solely because the employer did not provide a basic accommodation, such as screen-reading software, would that decision not amount to discrimination?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Similarly, if a caregiver of a severely-disabled child is denied a job simply because they requested FWAs or hybrid meeting options, when the role can reasonably accommodate these requests, should that not also be seen as an unjust barrier under WFL?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The Tripartite Guidelines on FWAs rolled out last December, are indeed a step forward.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, they raise an important question: if FWAs can be strongly encouraged, should we not go further and make FWAs a required reasonable accommodation for those with specific protected characteristics, particularly, PwDs or caregivers of vulnerable persons?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For PwDs and their caregivers, remote or hybrid work arrangements is very much welcomed due to their unique needs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This also is profitable for our labour pool.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Incorporating FWAs into the WFL as a legislated accommodation for PwDs and caregivers would send a clear and powerful message that inclusivity is not optional, but an essential principle.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As we explore other potential accommodations that balance the needs of employers with those of employees, it is critical that we act with urgency and intent.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Today's decisions will shape workplaces where those who need the most support are given the opportunity to thrive and where fairness is embedded in every aspect of our work culture.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Second, the Open Door Programme grant scoped as legislated reasonable accommodation.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This significantly reduce the financial burden of inclusive hiring.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: However, many companies may find the application process daunting due to administrative challenges.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: To address this, I urge MOM and MSF to collaborate with SG Enable to simplify and streamline the application process.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: By reducing administrative barriers and improving access to information, agencies can encourage more companies to take advantage of these grants, fostering a greater willingness to make reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For WFL to succeed, we must include education and training for hiring agents and managers.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Awareness of what constitutes discrimination, at every stage of employment, is critical.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: I will share two examples where two hiring officers have, unknowingly, discriminated against PwDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The first example, at the pre-employment stage, some deaf individuals have faced overt discrimination.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: For instance, one deaf applicant included a note in her CV requesting responses via email.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: After weeks without replies, she added a friend's phone number.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: When the hiring officer called the friend and learned the applicant was deaf, they responded, "In that case, we will delete her name from the list." As the role did not require hearing or speaking on the phone, this was a clear and unjust act of discrimination.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Here is a second example: a neurodivergent individual shared that his manager explicitly marked him down during a performance appraisal because he requested clarifications and step-by-step guidance on tasks.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: The markdown was based on the performance criterion of "ability to work independently with minimal supervision".

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: But requests for clarifications are common for neurodivergent individuals and should not be penalised.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: These programmes should aim to raise awareness and foster understanding among hiring agents and managers, about what constitutes discriminatory behavior towards PwDs.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Understandably, many may be unaware of what fair requests and reasonable accommodations entail.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: This also underscores the critical role of the Advisory on Reasonable Accommodation in ensuring the successful implementation of WFL.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Imagine constructing a state-of-the-art office building and declaring it open, yet failing to include a wheelchair ramp.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: How can we genuinely call the space "inclusive" or "equitable", if an entire group is excluded from ease of entrance?

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: As we advance WFL, let us ensure it becomes more than just a vision or a set of ideals.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: It must function as a practical, inclusive framework that truly works for everyone.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Embracing reasonable accommodations for PwDs will be a testament to our nation's shared commitment to equity and inclusivity.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Like a bridge that creates access, these accommodations open the doors to equal opportunities.

speaker: Miss Rachel Ong (West Coast)
text: Together, let us construct a bridge to workplace fairness; one that leaves no one behind and ensures everyone can cross to the other side comfortably.
, "That the Bill be now read a Second Time." –  .

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak in support of this Workplace Fairness Bill today.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is a significant milestone for a cause that is close to my heart.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Not only did I address this issue of fair employment practices in my maiden speech in Parliament nine years ago, I have raised two related Adjournment Motions on the topic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This Bill should be celebrated because, like the United Kingdom (UK), the Equality Act 2010, which I referenced in my 2021 Adjournment Motion speech on the "Strengthening the Singapore Core", this Bill centralises anti-discrimination laws in a single Act and will make the law easier to understand while strengthening protection in some situations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While this Bill will generally prohibit workplace discrimination on the basis of protected characteristics, such as sex, caregiving responsibilities, disability and mental health conditions, we must be clear that it prescribes minimum standards and not exhaustive benchmarks.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We should and must go beyond these minimum standards in order to promote a diverse workforce that is fairly treated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For the other roughly 5% of the complaint cases, may I ask: what is the employee characteristic that is allegedly discriminated against, which has not been covered by the proposed Bill?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In our unique system emphasising tripartism and harmonious labour relations, I am sure many would agree that employers should, nevertheless, pay careful attention to these potential fault lines even if they are not covered by the anti-discrimination laws in this Bill.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Second, the Bill sets a relatively low bar of merely preventing discrimination, which is defined as making an employment decision which adversely affects an individual.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is in contrast to equality legislation in the UK and Australia, which mandates an employer's duty to make reasonable adjustments for persons with disabilities (PwDs).

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If a business chooses to move its office premises from a wheelchair-accessible building to the upper floors of a shophouse without lift access, would it have discriminated against its wheelchair-bound employee under the proposed Bill?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Under the UK regime, the employer would quite certainly be obliged to consider if that employee's job function can be performed remotely from outside the office, under its legal duty to make reasonable adjustments.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If the latter, how would they be differentiated and structured?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, the practical bite of the anti-discrimination laws will depend largely how they are enforced and investigated.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: From the numerous provisions to protect complainants from retaliation, breach of professional conduct rules or ethics as well as civil and criminal liability, am I correct to understand that the authorities will generally rely on aggrieved employees to file a claim and pursue it through the prescribed process?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the authorities also be conducting active investigation and enforcement if it catches wind of potential infringements of anti-discrimination laws?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Especially for errant employers where the aggrieved employees find it futile to come forward?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If so, I hope the Commissioner for Workplace Fairness can be granted meaningful powers to conduct investigations and obtain documents on its own initiative, even outside the formal workplace discrimination claim, in the second piece of legislation that is expected to cover the procedural rights and processes.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I mentioned in my maiden speech in Parliament back in 2016, what is also key is to debunk any perception that the available opportunities are unequal and there is discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Yet there is bound to be some black sheep, even as many employers are committed to fair employment practices even without the need for legislation.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This enables the public to see that employers have been taken to task, what actions they have been penalised for.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It can also serve to guide the behaviour of other employers going forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If we want these anti-discrimination laws to have practical application for aggrieved employees, we ought to pay particular attention to the burden and standard of proof required to establish discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I noted, in my 2018 speech, that proving discrimination is "challenging".

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It is often difficult for employees to show that an adverse decision made against them, is due protected characteristics that they have, because any documentary records are usually kept by the employer organisation and such organisations will likely be advised by in-house counsel or external lawyers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Frivolous claims can be deterred by granting authorities the power to summarily strike out manifestly unmeritorious claims and requiring frivolous claimants to pay the costs of their dismissed action, in line with a tripartite committee's recommendation accepted by the Government.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Undoubtedly, the employer bears the burden of proving that a protected characteristic is a genuine job requirement, if it wishes to rely on the "genuine business need" exception.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The provision states that a protected characteristic is a genuine job requirement if, among other things, the job "cannot be reasonably performed" by an individual, unless they possess or lack the protected characteristic.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Consider the example of a hearing impaired individual and an audio production manager role - would the threshold be regarded as an impossibility?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What about an individual applying for a sales representative role focused on the Indonesian market, for instance, who does not read or speak Bahasa Indonesia but is willing to learn it?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a Member of Parliament in Toa Payoh East, I have encountered residents providing feedback about experiencing or perceiving discrimination at work or during job applications due to their race, wearing a tudung or needing to attend Friday prayers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In such cases, I typically refer them to TAFEP or advise them to contact TAFEP directly.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are highly sensitive and important issues for the Malay/Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Our handling of such issues is critical in maintaining multiracial and multi-religious harmony in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In my capacity as a TAFEP committee member, I have observed how TAFEP manages such cases.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It often comes down to open and sensitive communication between employers and employees, applicable not only to Malay/Muslim issues but also to other situations where employees and employers have differing needs and expectations.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: If both parties cannot reach a resolution, the employee can approach TAFEP.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: TAFEP will hear them out and help both parties better understand each other's perspectives, working towards a solution that meets both the employee's needs and the employer's business requirements.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For instance, I understand there was a case where an interviewer asked a jobseeker if she was willing to remove her tudung for work.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: TAFEP intervened in this case, and the employer clarified that it had no such requirement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It was prepared to offer the role to the jobseeker and allow her to wear the tudung at work.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: However, the jobseeker had already found another job opportunity by then.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So TAFEP separately identified gaps in the employer's hiring processes and worked with the employer to improve them.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This includes training interviewers to ask only job-related questions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These issues need to be managed even beyond the bill itself.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Regarding the Bill, I would like to understand the process if I am an affected employee.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Is the burden of proof on the employee?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would we need to wear a body camera, for example, to provide evidence?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I hope this legislation will simplify the process for legitimately affected employees to easily raise cases and will have adequate recourse and won't be deterred from coming forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: So, it is important to clarify when a job "cannot be reasonably performed", because job descriptions can sometimes be cleverly drafted to achieve a particular objective.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: During my Meet-the-People sessions over the years, I have encountered many individuals who felt that the jobs they were applying for, contained such bespoke or complicated prerequisites which suggested that the employer had already considered reserving the job for a particular foreign worker.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the trend of such complaints over the past five years since COVID-19 struck?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Could the Ministry of Manpower share some examples of how it “saw through” such patronising attempts to first advertise the job to locals? : Mr Speaker, since I am on the topic of exceptions, I am glad to see that express exceptions have been created for the two areas which I had focused on in my 2019 Adjournment Motion on tackling workplace and job discrimination.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What is the unemployment rate for persons that are 55 years old and above, compared to the unemployment rate for adults under that age?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Why is this age not pegged to our minimum retirement and re-employment ages, which have been adjusted upwards over the years?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: More fundamentally, is it not too blunt to prescribe a single age threshold to encourage the employment of older workers?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In particular industries, a 55-year-old might be deemed old and ordinarily less preferable than a younger worker.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In other industries however, a 55-year-old might still be in his or her prime and the exception should really apply to encourage the employment of even older workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In the more than 10 years that the Fair Consideration Framework (FCF) has been in force, how have we measured the success of the FCF in achieving its objectives?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What are the gaps that have been detected in the operation of FCF and how does the present workplace fairness reforms seek to fix that?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As a small population, we will require foreign manpower to augment and complement the local workforce, but not to substitute it.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One area that we can focus on more strongly is how we encourage and track the transfer of capabilities from foreign talent to local workers.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Having run programmes like the Capability Transfer Programme, can the Ministry shed some light on how have we gone about assessing the success of onshoring capabilities?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One final area that will be key in determining the success of this Workplace Fairness Legislation (WFL) is whether there is adequate avenue for recourse and relief for aggrieved employees.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Can an employer be directed to pay compensation to victimised employees?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But I would flag that the procedure should be as simplified as possible so that an aggrieved employee can navigate it without having to engage a lawyer.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As I had mentioned in this House back in 2018, I have heard from employees who have given up on legal action against employers because it is too expensive and troublesome.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Before I end, Mr Speaker, being on the TAFEP Committee, I would like to find out from MOM, given the extensive coverage on workplace fairness that will be ongoing if this Bill is passed, may I ask the Minister the extent of support for related agencies, especially TAFEP, in terms of manpower and other resources going forward, if this Bill is passed.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: But this Bill must be seen as a building block, rather than an end in itself.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We must continue to bear the principles underlying the Bill and go above and beyond the minimum legal obligations imposed, as our unique tripartite system is used to doing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My maiden speech in this 14th Parliament on 1 September 2020 focused on workplace discrimination of Singaporeans vis-a-vis foreign talent.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Job security has been a hot issue since the General Election (GE) in 2011.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Prior to that election, the Government gave out very large numbers of PRs, peaking at almost 80,000 new PRs in 2008 before reducing to the 30,000 a year today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There was widespread anger when the Government released the population White Paper in 2013, partly because many Singaporeans felt that the influx of new migrants had been a threat to their jobs and more migrants would worsen this trend.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Until today, many still feel the same way.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Workplace discrimination and anxieties over foreign workers, again, became a top concern during GE 2020, amid job losses during the COVID-19 pandemic.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In his National Day Message in 2021, then-Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong admitted that the Government has to adjust its policies to manage the quality, numbers and concentration of Work Pass holders.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: He later announced, at the National Day Rally, that the Fair Employment Guidelines would be enshrined into law.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has been more than three years since then.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Workplace Fairness Bill we are debating today is long awaited.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It begs the question as to why the Government has taken so long to table this Bill when it should be the Government's top concern to ensure that Singaporeans have fair access to employment opportunities.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP welcomes this Workplace Fairness Bill, which protects workers from discrimination on ground of 11 clearly designated, protected characteristics.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This should be the paramount goal of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And lastly, what are the plans to extend the coverage of the Bill to platform workers and expand the list of protected characteristics in future?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the years, we have heard many complaints on the ground from Singaporeans who feel aggrieved that foreigners have been preferred for jobs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP notes that nationality is one of the characteristics protected under clause 9 of the proposed Bill; and clause 22 says that it is not discrimination for an employer to make an employment decision that adversely affects an individual if that individual is neither a Singapore Citizen nor a PR of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is a clear indication that the Bill provides for preference to Singaporeans and PRs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, how did we reach a point where we need to explicitly state that preference for Singaporean workers are not considered discrimination?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When and how did Singaporeans lose their first right to jobs in their own country?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Why can the Bill not stipulate directly that all else being equal, Singaporeans should have the first right over a foreigner to any job in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government owes an answer to Singaporeans, especially those who have been displaced and underemployed in the last two decades.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And like the Minister has said, this Bill is not a panacea.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It has to be backed up by other policies that remove the causes or incentives for discrimination.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, one example is to ensure that there is no wage disparity between a Singaporean and a foreign worker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We can manage the level of wages in the economy to maintain our competitiveness, but we should never allow a wage disparity to exist that disadvantages the Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is the only way to stop employers from favouring cheaper foreign workers over Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: PSP welcomes quality foreign workers who have skillsets that are not readily available in Singapore to be recruited to enrich and complement our workforce, but not cheaper foreign workers who only displaces our more expensive Singaporean workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similarly, while age is stipulated as a protected characteristic in the Bill, this may not be enough to eliminate the temptation for employers to substitute older and more expensive Singaporean workers with cheaper foreign workers to boost the bottom line.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have to back up the Bill with additional measures to strengthen protection of our older workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These measures may take the form of job support subsidies for older workers, which can be funded by the foreign levies collected.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I will discuss how the exemptions granted may reduce the effectiveness of the new law.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Under clause 4(1) of the Bill, the Act will not apply to businesses with fewer than 25 workers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This same exemption is already used in the used in the Complementary Assessment Framework (COMPASS) system.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the Committee of Supply in 2023, I highlighted that this exemption could provide a potential loophole that will allow larger companies to set up subsidiaries that can discriminate based on nationality, for example, by employing one local and 24 foreign professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs).

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Alternatively, foreigners could partner locals to set up small companies to supply manpower to our bigger companies, hence depriving Singaporeans of good jobs in the bigger companies.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We have the same concerns about exempting contracts for service under clause 4(3) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This exemption means that a service buyer could include discriminatory provisions in his bid document or contract with the service provider.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, clauses 4(1) and 4(3) could potentially be used together by a big company to contract SMEs with less than 25 persons to supply it with Work Pass holders and even from one single nationality.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, we hope MOM will diligently monitor these exemptions and ensure that they are not abused.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the debate on the Platform Workers' Bill last September, I and other Members, including the Leader of the Opposition and Assoc Prof Jamus Lim, have spoken about platform workers potentially facing discrimination because of their CPF contributions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This concern is especially pertinent in the short-term until we reach a point where the majority of the workers available for platform work will need mandatory CPF.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Platform workers may now enjoy more legal protections under the Platform Workers Act, but they will not have access to the remedies available to employees under the Workplace Fairness Bill if they experience discriminatory treatment while working on the platforms.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Additionally, we find it hard to understand the intention of clause 17(3) of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Minister explain whether this clause 17(3) allows an employer to dismiss a worker A on the ground of the race or religion of A's husband?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Leader of the Opposition has also raised this yesterday and I look forward to a clearer explanation from the Minister later.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Work is fundamental in providing a person with meaning in life.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That is why I have spoken out repeatedly about job security and workplace fairness.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's policies should communicate to all employers in no uncertain terms that all else being equal, Singaporeans will have the first right to a job.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need additional policies to oblige employers to justify why a foreigner is favoured over a Singaporean when both have the same skills to do the same job.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For example, in Australia, employers can sponsor foreign workers only if they can demonstrate that they cannot find an Australian citizen or permanent resident with the skills and experience needed for the job.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Similarly, in Canada, most employers need to conduct a labour market impact assessment to determine that there is a need for a temporary foreign worker and that no Canandian citizens or permanent residents are available, before they can hire a temporary foreign worker.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This Bill is a landmarked piece of legislation for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I acknowledge the hard work put in by the Minister and his Ministry.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But its real worth is in substantially improving the job prospects of Singaporeans in general and protecting more vulnerable workers from workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If that is done, it will be a big step towards realising a harmonious and cohesive society.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have been actively engaging Singaporeans, especially in the West of Singapore for the past four years as a Non-Constituency Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A consistent message has emerged from these engagements.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is increasingly difficult for Singaporeans to find a job that commensurate with their skills and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It appears that rising under-employment amongst Singaporeans is a growing menace to us as a nation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government needs to do a lot more and not rest on its laurels by just focusing on the low unemployment numbers.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The low unemployment numbers may be camouflaging serious underemployment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A whole-of-Government approach is needed to reset our education, training, manpower and immigration policies so that Singaporeans can have stable that commensurate with their skills and aspirations.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must prevent under-employment from taking root in Singapore, or the Singapore we know today may become extinct in the near future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We must have a Parliament that heeds this message and a Government that implements effective manpower policies for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The Workplace Fairness Bill marks a significant step towards equality and inclusivity in our workforce.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: For more than a decade, various advocates within the Labour Movement, including fellow Labour Member, our brother, Mr Patrick Tay, have called for more to be done to level the playing field for our workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: More recently in 2021, the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) together with the Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF), called for more legislative measures to better protect our PMEs against age and nationality discrimination.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We are glad that our calls for stronger protections have been heeded.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: While necessary, legislation cannot be the only tool to tackle discrimination, especially when it concerns issues on race and religion.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We must recognise that these are sensitive issues that can impact our racial and religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: First, I will highlight the often-invisible cost of racial and religious discrimination to workers.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Second, I will speak on what more must be done to foster safer workplace cultures where sensitive issues involving race, language and religion are respectfully navigated.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Lastly, I will share my views on some issues raised by the Malay/Muslim community that have been covered by other Members in this debate.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: In 2020, NTUC's LabourBeat reported on Michael, a business consultant in his 40s who faced humiliation and mistreatment at work due to his ethnicity.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: With support from NTUC's U PME Centre, he was able to rebuild his confidence, secure a new job aligned with his career goals and even enjoy a 25% pay increase.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This story is a testament to the power of targeted support, but it also highlights that racial discrimination is still present in our workplaces.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This low reporting rate indicates that many workers feel disempowered or fear repercussions for speaking out.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: The workplace is a highly competitive environment where individuals spend a significant portion of their lives.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Many travel far from home to work here, contributing to Singapore's economic success.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It is only fair that their contributions are judged on merit, free from prejudice or unconscious bias.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, the complexities of racial and religious issues often result in genuine grievances being overlooked and dismissed.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Victims may be accused of using their race or religion as an excuse for poor performance, causing them to question their self-worth.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This silent killer, workplace discrimination, can infect and weaken the very fabric of our society.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: It sends a signal that our racial and religious harmony must be safeguarded with the utmost care.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: What more should be done to foster safer workplace cultures, where employers and employees respectfully navigate sensitive issues involving race, language and religion?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We must consider our changing workforce demographics, and the evolving complexities of workplace challenges.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: That is why, beyond the WFL, we will require a more holistic approach to foster safer workplace cultures upstream in order to stamp out prejudices and biases that can lead to disharmonious workplaces, even if they may not cross the legislative threshold to constitute an offence.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Here are my recommendations to foster safer workplace cultures.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: First, the Government should dedicate more resources to equip employers and HR practitioners to manage complex workplace disputes.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Training programmes should be enhanced to ensure practical ways in navigating differing perspectives on discrimination.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Second, ongoing education for employees and employers is essential to prevent unconscious bias and discrimination from taking root.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This includes fostering and engaging in dialogue that cultivate a culture of respect and understanding.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Third, workers must feel safe to voice their concerns without fear of retaliation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Strengthening mediation processes and offering confidential reporting mechanisms can help address grievances before they escalate.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Yesterday, Mr Faisal Manap raised two issues affecting our Muslim workers: namely, flexibility to participate in Friday prayers and flexibility to don the hijab while working.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Our workplaces are an important common space for workers from all walks of life to earn a living.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This diversity is a complex issue as different workers may choose to express their beliefs, practices and convictions differently.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Our union leaders understand the difficulties in balancing workers’ different needs for flexibility and accommodations, and work hard to support this diversity.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: We are glad that Mr Faisal Manap is appreciative of our unions’ efforts and highlighted that NTUC’s leaders had called for more understanding amongst employers to try to accommodate diverse needs where possible.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: However, we are concerned about the approach suggested to resolve these sensitive issues through discrimination claims under the legislation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: A better way is to handle the issue collectively and sensitively, involving tripartite partners in close dialogue.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This is not the first time that such issues have been surfaced and resolved harmoniously.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: This followed dialogues and close engagements with religious groups and public healthcare institutions, and demonstrates our ability to work through these matters in a constructive manner that promotes rather than erodes our religious harmony.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: To uphold our nation's social defence and ensure that every worker feels respected, valued and included, we must go further.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
