text: By equipping HR professionals, fostering inclusive workplace cultures and addressing discrimination proactively, we can build a workforce that truly reflects the values of meritocracy and fairness.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Singapore's continued safety and prosperity depend on our ability to safeguard the trust between our diverse communities.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman (Marine Parade)
text: Let us commit ourselves to this cause, ensuring that our workplaces are not only spaces for productivity but also bastions for respect and dignity.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I would just like to clarify whether, the two instances that I cited yesterday that are not covered by the law or the WFL.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: One of them is about allowing Muslim males to go for Friday prayers and the other one is the wearing of tudung for female Muslims.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Am I right to say that the Member disagrees that these two instances are supposed to be covered under WFL?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: I did not mention it that way, but I think what is important is that we can take these two issues together in a form of communications and addressing this in a dialogue, so that we can address this issue in a way to enhance productivity and enhance inclusivity in a workplace situation.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: That is the thing that I wanted to highlight.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: But what I am trying to say is, whether under the current Bill, which is going to be enacted soon, most probably, I just wanted to know whether he actually agrees that it should be covered under this legislation, this Bill, for the two instances that I mentioned?

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: It is something that, as what I mentioned, is being highlighted in the Malay/Muslim community because of the current issues.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: But the way and how we do it is actually through conversations, through communications and through addressing some of the issues highlighted by the employers and hearing what are the needs of their employees too.

speaker: Mr Mohd Fahmi Aliman
text: So, that is the gist of what I am trying to promote here – open conversations, open discussions, so that the workers will continue to be productive and not be impacted by all this.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Did I understand him correctly that he wanted privileges for Muslim men for Friday worship?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What about Muslim ladies, because they also go to mosques for worship?

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are all here trying to create a more equitable, a fairer society where we take into consideration all aspects of sex, race, nationality, PwDs, mental health and age.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, I am just trying to understand what his stand was when he put up this point yesterday.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And I will try my best to address it in my wrap-up speech later.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: So, I will be grateful for that clarification.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap
text: That is why I am asking on behalf of male Muslims.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, this Bill has been a long time in the making.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since the former Prime Minister announced the Government decision to proceed with such legislation at the National Day Rally in 2021, more than three years ago, the day has finally come, at least for the first part of the legislation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, it covers all stages of employment from pre-employment hiring, in-employment decisions to end-employment decisions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, when employers are assessed to have breached their obligations, there is a range of responses from financial penalties and corrective directions to state prosecution, with employers having recourse to the courts if necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my speech today, I would like to raise three questions related to the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We first understood that the anti-discrimination law was expected to be passed by the end of last year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When there was no indication by October last year that the law was being tabled, I was puzzled and filed a Parliamentary Question (PQ) about this for the November Sitting.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Ministry be more specific as to the various milestones and approximate target dates, so that we can better understand why it will take so much time?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My second question arises from the scope of the Act, that is, what situations are covered or not covered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note from clause 4(3) that the Act does not cover contracts for service, that is, those who are engaged under arrangements that make them independent contractors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While I do not disagree with this, I wish to highlight ground feedback I have received about some unscrupulous employment practices.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A resident told me that he had worked for his employer for years and when he was nearing retirement age, his work arrangement with the employer was converted from the status of employee to a contract for service, that is, he was re-hired as an independent contractor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This was despite the fact he was working at the same tasks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a change in status from employee to independent contractor would deprive the worker of significant protections, such as CPF contributions, work injury compensation insurance and soon, from the provisions of the Workforce Fairness Act as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is not acceptable as such a practice is tantamount to discrimination on the grounds of age.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is the Ministry tracking such situations of potential bullying of older workers, and if so, what is being done?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My last question relates to what the Bill calls “protected characteristics”.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These 11 protected characteristics range from age, sex and nationality to marital status, race and mental health condition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My query relates to the pre-employment stage, that is, when the employer is deciding whether or not to hire an individual.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Fundamentally, my question is this: what exactly are the restrictions on what the employer can or cannot do?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the Bill states that the employer should not make an adverse employment decision based on any of the protected characteristics, it is silent on how the employment processes need to change.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, is the employer permitted to ask any questions about the protected characteristics?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, it is common in Singapore to see pre-employment forms asking potential hires for their marital status, race and whether they have been ever treated for any mental health condition.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: During hiring interviews, women especially are often asked about their caregiving responsibilities or potential parenthood plans.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Regarding what sorts of questions cannot or should not be asked during hiring interviews, a brief look at some other jurisdictions is useful.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At one end of the spectrum, some jurisdictions, such as South Korea and Denmark, legally prohibit employers from asking for information on marital status and race.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Mid-way in the spectrum would be other jurisdictions, such as the United States (US) and the UK, where questions about some characteristics are not permitted at all, for example, on disability and health.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, for other characteristics, such as pregnancy or parenthood plans, employers are merely advised not to ask those questions, as such questions could be considered to be evidence of discrimination.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is the Ministry’s intention to prohibit certain lines of questioning or is the intention merely to discourage such questions?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will there be, for instance, subsidiary legislation covering prohibited questions and what the consequences will be if they are asked?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For questions that are to be discouraged, this change itself will involve overhauling long-standing hiring norms.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How will MOM work with employers to adjust their hiring practices and to monitor whether these practices have indeed changed?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This express statement is something that deeply resonates with me as a minority woman.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Many Singaporean minorities, including myself, have experienced being in work situations where the majority of their co-workers and, sometimes, even their superiors have preferred to communicate in Mandarin.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In these cases, they have little regard for the people around them who may not be able to understand what they are saying.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This kind of behaviour is isolating and goes against Singapore’s core commitment to multiculturalism.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I wish to thank the Government for being clear that this kind of discrimination, if performed in connection with the acts set out in Part 4 of this proposed law, is totally unacceptable. : Notwithstanding my particular support for this aspect of the Bill, I have a few clarifications for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: My main clarifications in my speech are on the definition of “sex” as it is set out in clauses 8(c) and 10 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A person’s gender identity and expression, as well as their sexuality, are a part of who they are.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: They are not lifestyle choices that can be changed on a whim.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: While the proposed law supports individuals who have undergone sex re-assignment procedures, it seems to ignore the reality that the transition from one gender to another is something that happens over time and involves more than just surgical changes.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Sometimes, individuals may not even choose to undergo surgical procedures.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is a complex process and it involves medical, psychological and social aspects.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Individuals in the process of transitioning, or who choose not to surgically transition, can also be susceptible to discriminatory practices in the workplace.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Members of the arts community who are also members of the LGBTQ+ community have told me that they feel very concerned about the additional exclusions at clause 10(2) of this Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: These exclusions could have the effect of reiterating the fact that characteristics which are relevant to the community will resolutely not have the protection of this law.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This could in fact signal to the wider population, as well as employers, that discrimination on the basis of one’s sexuality and gender identity, are not sufficiently serious or valid concerns.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Taken to an extreme, some might interpret this as the Government condoning this kind of workplace discrimination.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: It could also inadvertently signal to employers that such discriminatory practices will go largely unpunished.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: This is not the only place where we see a similar kind of signalling in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Speaking as someone who actually does have a husband of a different race, this was slightly alarming for me to read in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I understand that given the prescriptive approach that has been adopted by the Government in this piece of legislation, certain lines have to be drawn and clear positions have to be elucidated.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To put it another way, when lists are made, there will always be questions on why certain things are included and others are left out.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To an extent, this is just something inherent in the structure of the legislation that has been adopted.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I think most members of the public and Members of this House can understand that.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But that being said, it is important too that the specific wording in the Bill does not send out unintended messages that seem to actually endorse certain acts of discrimination.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: To this end, it would be good if the Minister could explain the basis behind the explanatory note on clause 17 and on how members of the public are expected to interpret it.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Yesterday, I note that the Minister has explained and mentioned that the acts that are described in the explanatory note would be caught by the Tripartite Guidelines on Fair Employment Practices (TGFEP) and just not by this Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: But notwithstanding his explanation, I would like to ask, was it then necessary to include an example like this in the Bill?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Could the explanatory note have been clearer that such acts are very much discriminatory, even if they are not covered by this Bill?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Coming back to the definition of sex, very recently, this House debated the repeal of section 377A of the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: In connection with this, many Members on both sides of the House reiterated their views that discriminatory behaviour towards people on account of their sexuality should simply not be tolerated.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, I do not think at all that the Government intends to send the message to the LGBTQ+ community that discrimination against them is in any way permissible.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I was also heartened to hear the Minister yesterday say that no one would be turned away with their workplace grievances just because they do not happen to be covered by the Bill.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister seems to have taken a very strong approach towards ensuring that tolerance is displayed by employers and by members of the public.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: On one level, this is a very logical way to proceed.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: However, we should not forget that it is also possible for discrimination to exist in the absence of formal complaints.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The report Discrimination and Harassment in the Workplace: The Lived Experiences of Singapore LGBTQ+ Individuals, raises some notable feedback.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: However, the report also noted that among the participants who had experienced discrimination and harassment, only a very small number had actually reported their experiences to their respective companies, to MOM or to TAFEP.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Some of the reasons for this included a fear of retaliation, social stigma and the expectation of little support if reports were actually made.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: We can see how this fear creates a harmful loop.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Victims remain unheard, leading those in positions of authority to mistakenly believe that there are no issues of concern.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: As a result, protections remain inadequate and those facing workplace discrimination continue to suffer quietly.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: So, my questions for the Minister are these: first, Did the Ministry take into account the research and feedback from the ground which indicate that LGBTQ+ individuals tend to under-report incidents of workplace discrimination and harassment?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If so, how then was the decision arrived at, to exclude sexuality and gender identity from the protected characteristic of “sex”?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Is the Minister able to provide any assurances that discrimination against employees on the basis of their gender identity and sexuality, will not be tolerated by the Ministry?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, will the Minister consider including specific protections, templates and resources for LGBTQ+ individuals through TAFEP and the TGFEP?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: Will any measures be put in place to ensure that reporting systems are accessible, trusted and effective for LGBTQ+ persons?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: The Minister yesterday alluded to updates being made to the TGFEP, so I look forward to hearing his further explanations and clarifications later.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: I would also like to ask if any measures would be put in place to ensure that reporting systems are accessible, trusted and effective for LGBTQ+ persons.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: For example, would the Ministry work with LGBTQ+ groups on the ground to conduct training for TAFEP and other frontline MOM staff to ensure that cases of discrimination are dealt with seriously and professionally, and to encourage reporting of such incidents, when they do take place?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If so, will a similar reconsideration of clauses 8(c) and 10 also take place?

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: A number of countries, including the UK, Australia and New Zealand have codified provisions against workplace discrimination based on gender identity and sexuality.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas (Nominated Member)
text: If we in Singapore were to change our position in future, we would certainly not be alone in doing so.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill signifies a significant step towards ensuring that our workplaces are not only productive but also inclusive, compassionate and fair.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: One in seven individuals in Singapore experience mental health challenges in their lifetime.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In the workplace, this often translates to stigma, reduced opportunities and hesitance to seek help.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Beyond the personal toll, mental health issues have a significant economic impact.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Such barriers affect individuals and hinder workforce morale, efficiency and overall economic growth.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Therefore, addressing mental health in the workplace is a moral responsibility and an economic imperative.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These measures create a much-needed safety net for workers, encouraging equitable treatment and reducing stigma.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: However, Sir, I do have some concerns and questions about the Bill, particularly regarding our mental health provisions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What diagnostic criteria or medical certifications are required for a mental health condition to qualify as a protected characteristic?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers and employees need clarity to avoid disputes over whether a condition is eligible for protection.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask because mental health conditions vary significantly from chronic disorders like schizophrenia, to temporary conditions such as acute stress.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Without a clear criteria, confusion or inconsistencies could arise.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As an example, an employee with an anxiety might present a certificate from a general practitioner, while any other with a similar condition may seek a psychiatrist diagnosis.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Ensuring clarity in what is accepted is crucial to avoid unfair outcomes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How can employers assess whether a mental health condition genuinely affects an employee's ability to perform safety critical roles?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers must navigate a fine line between ensuring workplace safety and avoiding discrimination.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask simply because certain industries, for example, in aviation or healthcare, or even construction, may involve high risk tasks where safety concerns are paramount.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers need clear guidance or guidelines to make balanced and reasonable decisions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As an example, we can have a construction worker who has severe anxiety and might require temporary re-assignment to lower-risk duties.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill ensures such decisions are grounded in genuine safety concerns rather than bias.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The third revolves around the grievance processes and retaliation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The question is, what mechanisms are in place to ensure grievance handling processes are unbiased and transparent.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employees may mistrust internal process if they are entirely employer driven, undermining the Bill's intent.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask simply because employers, especially SMEs, might lack the resources or expertise to set up impartial grievance system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As an example, if an employee files a complaint against their manager and, because it is an SME, the same manager may oversee the grievance process and this creates a clear conflict of interest.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Thus, we need to establish independent reviews to mitigate such concerns.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: How also will this Bill protect employees from subtle forms of retaliation after they raise a mental health related grievance?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employees often fear indirect retaliation, such as being excluded from promotions or sidelined in projects, even if overt discrimination is addressed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask simply because subtle retaliation is harder to detect and prove, making robust protections vital.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Bill explicitly prohibits such acts and provides penalties for violations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As an example, an employee who discloses that he or she may have post-traumatic stress disorder and subsequently notices a drop in their responsibilities despite consistent performance, might suspect retaliation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers must demonstrate that such changes are justified and not punitive.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: My fourth point is regarding privacy and confidentiality.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: What safeguards ensure that employees' mental health information remains confidential during the grievance investigations or workplace discussions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Breaches of privacy could discourage employees from disclosing their conditions, and we want them to come forward, but this may undermine the Bill's intent.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I ask simply because sensitive information about mental health must be handled carefully to avoid stigma and protect employees' dignity.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Employers must implement robust confidentiality protocols during investigations or accommodations.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: As an example, if an HR team inadvertently shares details about an employee's mental health condition with co-workers, it could lead to workplace gossip, further alienating the individual.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I am encouraged by how this Bill aligns with our broader efforts to strengthen mental health advocacy in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Workplace Fairness Bill is not a standalone initiative.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It builds on the foundation of community programmes, public awareness campaigns and mental health education.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Last Sunday, I had the opportunity through the People's Action Party (PAP) Mental Health Group to hold its first meet-up session of 2025, bringing together passionate individuals and organisations that are dedicated in advancing mental health initiative.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some of them include Silver Ribbon (Singapore), SCMH, Calm Collective, Campus Psy, Limitless, Growthbeans and many more.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is inspiring to see so many shared aspirations among the community to make mental health a national priority.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Together, I believe we are driving impactful change and this Bill plays a critical role in shaping that transformation.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a declaration of our values as a nation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Pope Francis said, and I quote, “Work is fundamental to the dignity of a person.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It gives one the ability to maintain oneself, one's family, and to contribute to the growth of one's own nation." The Workplace Fairness Bill matters because it opens doors for more persons to access work opportunities regardless of background and personal characteristics.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As important, it upholds every person's right to be treated fairly and with respect because it strengthens protections against discrimination and empowers workers to seek remedial action from their employers directly without fear of retaliation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: On these grounds, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: I also seek clarity on how the Bill would deliver sustained positive impact for less-advantaged communities that have the odds stacked up against them in the job market and the workplace.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: First, clause 28 of the Bill outlines the prohibition against retaliation.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister explain what constitutes, I quote, "subjecting the employee to any other detriment in relation to the employee's employment".

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Next, the Bill outlines what constitutes direct workplace discrimination in respect of the protected characteristics.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: However, the Bill leaves out what are reasonable accommodations that must be put in place to facilitate employment outcomes.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Clarity on the provision of reasonable accommodations would pave the way for more Singaporeans to be purposefully engaged in work, to develop viable careers and livelihood and to contribute economically to Singapore.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Fellow Parliamentarians, such as Mayor Ms Denise Phua, Mr Ong Hua Han and Miss Rachel Ong spoke extensively yesterday about the need for reasonable accommodations for persons with disabilities and offered sound suggestions to nudge more employers into action.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, could the Minister outline how the Ministry plans to normalise for employers to make reasonable accommodations that cater to the different needs of different demographics in the workforce?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such expansion would be in tandem with Singapore's Enabling Masterplan 2030 that gives a big push for inclusive hiring.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Next, advocates for PwDs such as Po Chien who I spoke with had surfaced concern about less-enlightened employers working around the law by asking for a candidate's National Service status or refusing to accept reasonable accommodations.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such concern is shared by those impacted by clause 10 of the Bill on the protected characteristics for sex where characteristics such as sexual orientation and gender identity were excluded.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These communities seek assurance that the Ministry would make every effort to guard against indirect methods of discriminating and protect those whose employment opportunities are undermined as a result.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Could the Minister share the recourse available to an individual with grounds to suspect that he or she has been discriminated by an employer because of their disability or sexual orientation or gender identity?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: What measures would the Ministry consider putting in place to deter such forms of discrimination?

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Nonetheless, I note that platform work arrangement is excluded from the Bill.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This is despite the efforts to differentiate platform workers from other self-employed workers because of the employee-like characteristics of platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They became platform workers because of the limitations that they have.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: They asked if the Bill could be extended to cover platform workers and protect platform workers against discrimination by platform algorithms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Because the Platform Workers Act imposes financial obligations on platform operators, these platform workers worry that platform operators would favour workers the operators deem as more productive and thus tighten control on who is allowed to onboard the platform and to participate in platform work.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such control is typically executed by platform algorithms that manage platform job allocation, fares and supervision.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, biases or preferences introduced deliberately or inadvertently by operators or picked up and internalised by platform algorithms would factor into the platform's algorithmic decision-making that could consistently deprioritise a particular worker in job allocation and/or fares or prioritise some workers over others.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such actions hurt the livelihoods of affected platform workers.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Workers ask if this Bill would grant them the right and avenue to seek fairness.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In the debate on the Platform Workers Bill, I had recommended for the Government to require platform operators to apply AI Verify to the platform algorithms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Doing so would motivate platform operators from the get-go to design and build artificial intelligence (AI) systems that are aligned with the 11 AI ethics principles.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from platform work, technology has also evolved recruitment practices.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: It is now common for companies to advertise their job postings on social media platforms.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To maximise advertising spend, recruiters would typically set limitations on the target audience receiving the job post.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This inadvertently narrows the audience for the job post to certain segments of the population.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In the absence of guardrails, employers could target by options that describe or relate to the protected characteristics.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such measures matter to Singapore's push for non-discrimination and fairness in a digital economy.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To prepare for this debate, I had spoken with different stakeholders and members.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Many had suggested for efforts to be directed to educate and equip managers and human resource practitioners because these individuals would be much involved in implementing the Bill at the workplace.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Although TAFEP and tripartite bodies have been active in educating the public on fair employment and hiring practices, there are employers that are less familiar with TAFEP's work and the discussions leading up to the drafting of this Bill.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These employers might have missed or deliberately ignored TAFEP's messages and thus would not have impressed upon their managers and HR team the importance of fair workplace practices.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These employers could also continue to hold on to stereotypes that perpetuate biases and unfair workplace practices.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To give a sense of the potential size of challenge of dismantling such stereotypes and biases, allow me to share a personal example from my capacity as a unionist.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: To this day, I have union members who were told to terminate their union membership if they accepted a promotion to executive roles.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This was told to them by their manager or HR.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: These management and HR had also communicated to staff members that executives cannot join the union.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Such myths have been widely propagated in the hospitality sectors where I am now serving in a unionist capacity.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, I cannot overstate the need for the Government to be relentless in its efforts to level the awareness and implementation capabilities of managers and HR practitioners.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Some of us might have caught Wicked, a recent movie release and the highest-grossing film adaptation of a Broadway musical.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: Allow me to share a quote from Jon M Chu, Wicked's director.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: He said, "Creating the set was one of the most enlightening and beautiful processes I have ever gone through" adding, "You need accessibility, not just when we are on set behind the scenes, but you need to present accessibility in Oz itself." I commend Mr Chu.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: His mindset and approach must be the desired states which the Workplace Fairness Bill is seeking to steer employers, colleagues and employees to embrace and aspire towards.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: As important, it is a beacon of hope and resilience for less-advantaged communities.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC and our unions have been championing fair and inclusive workplaces.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill gives us firmer ground to work closely with employers and tripartite stakeholders to pave the way for more workplaces to be fair and inclusive.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill also gives individuals the courage to surface discriminatory practices that they might experience or come across.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: NTUC and the unions stand ready to support members in these situations.

speaker: Ms See Jinli Jean (Nominated Member)
text: In closing, I call upon this House and fellow Singaporeans to unite in purpose and action so that all working people, regardless of their background, can be empowered to uphold that dignity to their right of work.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended at 4.10 pm until 4.30 pm.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, the Workplace Fairness Bill is an important milestone in Singapore's journey to update employment practices and improve the work environment.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These measures are necessary to enable more PwDs to find, maintain and advance in employment.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For those who wish to work, they should be encouraged and supported in their endeavours to earn their own living and gain financial independence.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many PwDs want to participate in the workforce, make use of their skillsets and education and contribute to our economy.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Workplace accommodation will benefit employers too, as a more diverse and inclusive workplace can add benefits to businesses.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Ministry's responses to prior feedback on indirect discrimination highlighted its concerns over the wider legal obligations for employers and potential uncertainty for both employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry consider this issue from another angle, that legislation is necessary to minimise such workplace uncertainties?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Presently, affected employees face the uncertainty of whether the indirect discrimination they experience would be taken seriously, which results in unreported cases.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There are grey areas where errant employers exhibit a range of indirect discriminatory behaviours.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The number of cases of discrimination, direct and indirect, are under-reported.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness Final Report took note of this.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Under Part IV of the section on Recommendations, paragraph 19, I quote, "Some employees may hesitate to come forward to report workplace discrimination or harassment within the company or to MOM or TAFEP, out of fear of subsequently being disadvantaged in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This sentiment was raised by participants during the 2020-2021 Conversations on Singapore Women's Development.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In addition, the MOM Fair Employment Practices Survey 2022 showed that only one in three employees who experienced workplace discrimination sought help." In August 2022, the gender equality group, AWARE in partnership with a consumer research company Milieu Insight, conducted a comprehensive survey on workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: They polled about 1,000 respondents on their experiences of workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The Ministry has stated that it is worried about employee-employer relationship becoming more legalistic if it starts prohibiting indirect discrimination.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As it is now, many employees are afraid of reporting the discrimination they face.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Most employees would seek to resolve the issue internally through internal channels and avenues, such as by reporting the issue to their manager or the HR department and try to resolve the issue amicably first.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: This is why it is important to mandate mediation first, before further action, such as litigation, can be taken.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: As for the issue of reasonable accommodations in the workplace, the Ministry can consider referencing comparative legislation and studying the experience of other countries.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, the US Department of Labor has established reasonable accommodation as a legal concept with clear criteria.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Many jurisdictions' laws also include the intertwined concept of "undue burden" where employers are not required to grant accommodation that impose "undue burden”.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, employers are protected from making accommodation which they cannot make with reasonable resource allocation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In Singapore, employers can approach MOM and disability organisations, such as SG Enable, Disabled People's Association, Autism Resource Centre (Singapore), Serving People with Disabilities and the Movement for the Intellectually Disabled for assistance and guidance on reasonable accommodation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Ministry consider providing greater incentives to encourage employers to proactively work with these organisations to support staff who are PwDs?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Reasonable accommodation is essential and necessary for PwDs to perform their jobs and is not a matter of personal preferences.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, blind persons need screen readers, deaf people need written communication, autistics need environments that accommodate their sensory sensitivity.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, it is important to recognise that by issuing an advisory instead of legislation on reasonable accommodation, employers would interpret them as optional provisions, when, in fact, they are necessary and indispensable means for PwDs to perform their daily tasks.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Without reasonable accommodation, PwDs are disadvantaged at every stage of the employment process.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, wheelchair users who are denied interviews because the venue of the interview is not wheelchair accessible.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Therefore, the denial of such essential reasonable accommodation would constitute an "adverse employment decision" as defined in the Workplace Fairness Final Report.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: There is more work to be done to build greater inclusion in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Hence, I would like to conclude with my full support for the Bill.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, the Workplace Fairness Bill 2024 represents a significant milestone in Singapore's commitment to creating equitable workplaces.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill codifies principles that have long been championed under the TGFEP, giving them legal weight and enforceability.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By addressing workplace discrimination, it sends a strong message that such discriminatory practices have no place in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: A 2022 Harvard Business Review article highlights that organisations prioritising fairness can achieve up to a 26% increase in productivity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: More than a reflection of our shared values of inclusivity and fairness, this Bill demonstrates how fairness is integral to enhancing business competitiveness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I also like that the Bill achieves a commendable balance between promoting inclusivity and addressing the practical realities of businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By allowing smaller businesses more time to adapt, it ensures workplace fairness becomes a shared responsibility across businesses of all sizes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Section 8 of the Bill also provides vital protections for vulnerable groups, including older employees, women with caregiving responsibilities and PwDs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: According to a recently released Singapore Business Federation's National Business Survey 2024, while business outlook has improved slightly, only 26% of businesses are confident about economic improvement in the year ahead, with 22% of businesses expecting conditions to worsen.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Rising manpower costs, cited as the top challenge by 66% of businesses, further strain their ability to invest in fair employment practices.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: SMEs face heightened challenges as they navigate rapid global changes while trying to sustain their operations with limited resources.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   First, implementing the measures outlined in this Bill comes with costs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Setting up grievance handling systems, for example, requires businesses to train staff, create reporting mechanisms and document complaints.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, employers may also hesitate to hire individuals requiring significant accommodations, fearing operational disruptions or additional costs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This reluctance could inadvertently hinder the inclusion of those most in need of workplace fairness policies.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: While this safeguards opportunities for Singaporeans, it can create challenges for industries experiencing acute talent shortages.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, in the technology sector, where roles such as software engineers, cybersecurity experts and AI specialists are in high demand, the limited local talent pool may lead to significant project delays and missed business opportunities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Fourth, the anti-retaliation provisions under section 28 are crucial to protecting employees who raise legitimate grievances.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These include the Fair Consideration Framework, implementing flexible work arrangements and enhanced parental leave guidelines.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Adding new compliance obligations could stretch their resources further, particularly for businesses without dedicated HR functions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To address these concerns while supporting the Bill's objectives, I propose eight recommendations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: First, we need a clear and comprehensive implementation framework.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is vital to retain the TAFEP's role as the primary point of contact for workplace fairness complaints.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Over the years, TAFEP has successfully championed conciliation, education and mindset shifts, earning the trust of both employers and workers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: MOM's statutory enforcement powers, while necessary, should remain a last resort.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: My concern is the transition to this new framework may create public confusion.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Employees may bypass TAFEP and approach MOM prematurely, undermining the conciliation-first approach.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Employers, on the other hand, may fear immediate enforcement actions without being given an opportunity for mediation.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To address these concerns, I propose a comprehensive public education campaign, working together with chambers and trade associations, to clarify the process: TAFEP as the first point of contact, mediation as the second step and MOM's intervention as a final recourse for unresolved disputes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Possible feedback mechanisms could also be set up for employers and employees to share their experiences with the new legislation, informing future refinements of the Bill over time.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Second, for the Workplace Fairness Bill to be effective, HR personnel must be equipped with the necessary skills to implement fair workplace practices effectively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I propose that TAFEP collaborate with the Institute for Human Resource Professionals (IHRP) to establish a robust framework for accrediting HR capabilities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Under this model, IHRP would serve as the standards and accreditation hub, while Institutes of Higher Learning, trade associations and chambers as well as training providers act as deployment spokes.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: To support this, IHRP, in partnership with TAFEP, could issue jointly branded skills badges.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These badges would serve as formal accreditation, demonstrating that HR personnel have been trained and are equipped with the knowledge and skills to implement workplace fairness policies effectively.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Third, to address concerns about the anti-retaliation provisions and to better support both employees and businesses, the Minister could consider introducing clearer definitions of "good faith" to prevent misuse of the provisions.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It is important to clarify what constitutes a failure to fulfil contractual obligations or subjecting an employee to detriment in employment, as well as outline the relative burdens of proof for all parties.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Including penalties for frivolous complaints and allowing employers to take documented disciplinary actions unrelated to complaints would help maintain fairness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, MOM could enhance TAFEP’s role to filter out frivolous claims during the initial triage process, streamlining the grievance resolution process and minimising undue burdens on businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This approach ensures that all businesses contribute to workplace fairness while considering their unique capacities.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Forward-looking SMEs, particularly those with 25 or fewer employees, that demonstrate exemplary workplace fairness practices and implementing them ahead of time, should be recognised and publicised.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: And the Tripartite Alliance Awards could be a useful platform for this.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond recognition, SMEs could be rewarded with tangible incentives, creating a balanced approach that includes not just the "stick" of compliance but also the "carrot" of acknowledgment and support.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Fifth, while MOM’s enforcement framework already categorises breaches into "low", "moderate" and "high" severity levels, the distinctions between these categories remain unclear to businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Providing detailed guidelines on what constitutes each level of severity would offer greater clarity and confidence to employers.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, prioritising education over penalties, particularly for first-time breaches, would allow businesses to adapt in time while maintaining deterrence for repeat or severe violations.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Sixth, simplified compliance reporting should be introduced to ease administrative strain on SMEs.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Pre-approved templates tailored for SMEs could reduce administrative overhead and help smaller firms navigate the new requirements more efficiently.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Seventh, financial support is essential in fostering inclusive workplaces.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Government has already demonstrated commendable foresight with initiatives such as the Job Redesign Grant, Open Door Programme and Enabling Employment Credit, which help businesses accommodate seniors, PwDs through workplace modifications and job redesign.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: However, there is a continued need to shift mindsets and build capacity for inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I would therefore like to propose expanding grants to support diversity training, grievance system implementation and inclusive hiring practices.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the Government could co-fund anti-discrimination training programmes for HR personnel and provide subsidies for setting up grievance systems, particularly for smaller businesses.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, targeted measures are needed for industries facing acute manpower shortages.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: This would help these sectors address their constrained talent pools without compromising the broader principles of workplace fairness.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: These voices are important and their advocacy highlights the need for continued dialogue and progress toward greater inclusivity.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: The Workplace Fairness Bill represents a significant first step in codifying anti-discrimination measures.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: It establishes a foundational framework that can evolve to address broader concerns in the future.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: Expanding protections prematurely, without addressing implementation challenges, could create unintended uncertainties for both employers and employees.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: By focusing on practical and actionable measures today, this Bill lays the groundwork for future enhancements, paving the way for a more inclusive workforce as society and businesses adapt and progress together.

speaker: Mr Mark Lee (Nominated Member)
text: I look forward to continued collaboration to address these concerns in the journey ahead.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I have been speaking up in favour of anti-discrimination legislation in this House several times over the years, including the very first Sitting of this term of Government in September 2020.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think there has been broad consensus, both on the characteristics that have been identified, as well as the exceptions carved out.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In dialogues I have had with women's groups over the years, one of the common issues they face in returning to the workforce is that employers are likely not to employ them because of concerns about their age and expected caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now that it will be prohibited to discriminate on these characteristics, they may have better opportunities to return to the workforce.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Likewise, older workers who are moving between jobs and face difficulty with younger, less experienced candidates being hired ahead of them may now also have express protection under the law.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I acknowledge that the Government and the unions have done a good job of encouraging workplace fairness over the years, including with the Tripartite Guidelines, but these have generally had the most fight with employers seeking EPs for foreign employees.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The MOM's denial of new work pass applications is already a potent stake against employers whose businesses depend heavily on foreign workers, and these employers had to become extra careful in ensuring they give Singaporeans fair consideration first.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will continue to be the case even with the new legislation.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The provisions in this Bill are unlikely to surprise multinational employers, particularly those from the West, where anti-discrimination legislation is quite common.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, many of these companies already have anti-discrimination provisions as part of their internal policies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would suggest though, that assistance be provided to local employers, including SMEs, on compliance with these provisions and in particular, the requirements of sections 25 to 27 of the new Bill that require employers to put in place fair employment practices.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I know a number of my colleagues have spoken in favour of recognising indirect discrimination as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think it is important to acknowledge that indirect discrimination exists, although these may be more difficult to establish in court.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: An example is where a person puts out characteristics for a job that may favour some groups over others, such as say a requirement for fair skin or curly hair.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As a starting point, the current legislation does make reference to some forms of indirect discrimination, one of the most common being irrelevant language requirements, which is essentially indirect racial discrimination.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Additionally, there is nothing in the legislation that prevents a court finding as a fact that a particular requirement may amount to discrimination under one of the protected characteristics.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my view, the current legislation may be used to deal with such discrimination, for example, under section 19(1), since they would give an advantage or disadvantage to certain races or nationalities.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I think these types of indirect discrimination can be left to the court to determine as and when the situation arises, although if common threats arise, such as in relation to the irrelevant language requirements, then the legislation can be modified to give express protection on these matters.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: As with any new legislation, there will likely be a spike in complaints when the legislation comes out and likely, some employers will be taken to task.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, once people get comfortable with and understand the obligations under the law, there will likely be a cultural shift and change in mentalities amongst both employers and employees, which I believe is healthy in the long run.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: As someone deeply engaged in senior policy, I have witnessed first-hand the challenges that some of our seniors face in the workplace.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Many have the experience, wisdom and resilience to contribute meaningfully, yet some are unfairly sidelined.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This Bill represents a bold step toward changing that reality.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: A senior construction project manager came to my Meet-the-People Session for help recently.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Despite decades of service and a stellar record, he struggled to find work after his company downsized, even after we spent months tapping on our extensive network to help him find a job. “Am I too old to matter?” he asked.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It reflects the silent battle some of our seniors face daily – not against a lack of ability, but against prejudice.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our seniors want to work and they deserve the chance.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Ageism is a hidden barrier that deprives our society of valuable skills and creates a culture of exclusion.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Without more action, we risk wasting the potential of our seniors, losing their contributions to our economy and our shared future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This Bill takes practical, meaningful steps to address these challenges.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The PAP Senior Group supports this law because real changes happens through practical, step-by-step progress.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This law avoids overreaching, which can lead to defensive HR practices, frivolous lawsuits, or even job losses as companies move overseas.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Just look at the controversies surrounding diversity, equity and inclusion, or DEI, in America.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The PAP Senior Group will work closely with the Government to ensure that this law is properly implemented.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: We can afford to take practical steps towards progress because we have been building on decades of senior-friendly policies by successive PAP governments, which includes, just to recap, reskilling initiatives like SkillsFuture Mid-Career schemes preparing our seniors for evolving industries, incentives for employers to hire seniors and encourage the creation of age-friendly workplaces, a very tight foreign manpower policy prioritising local employment and investments in healthcare, preventive care and fitness, helping our seniors remain active and ready for work.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: The PAP Government have always championed respect, regard and recognition for our seniors and this Bill continues that legacy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: While this Bill is a major step forward, there are also areas we can consider further action over the coming years.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Let us survey seniors more extensively, not just those who have exited the workforce, but also those who are trying to re-enter the workforce or those who deem themselves unemployed, to better understand the nature of discrimination.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Second, we should also monitor HR practices to ensure that indirect discrimination does not rise as a response to this law and this requires monitoring, indirect discrimination by sector, industry and company size.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Third, improving how we measure workers' well-being and mental health.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our tripartite partners can build a consensus on how the mental, emotional and physical health are evaluated through affordable psychometric and fitness tests.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This will reduce the scope of disputes over what constitutes discrimination.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Our Civil Service should, at all levels, implement the Bill in both form and spirit, and ensure that their outsourced HR service providers meet the same standard.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Fifth, share learnings from TADM and the Employment Claims Tribunals (ECT).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Given that the law calls for TADM and ECT to take the lead in fighting indirect discrimination, regular updates from both groups to Parliament and the public will help us adapt policies effectively.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Sixth, and the last, plan for the future.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Start a review in three years to ensure this Bill remains relevant amidst rapidly changing geopolitics, trade-flow and technological changes.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It will also allow us to factor our seniors' better health, as Healthier SG bears fruits.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: This Bill opens doors, but it is up to all of us to walk through them together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Prioritise your health because an active body fuels an active mind.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Believe in your ability to contribute, you are not just workers; you are mentors, leaders and role models for younger generations.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Choosing inclusiveness is not just good policy, it is good business, because a diverse workplace brings experience, balance and strength.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is a statement about who we are as a society.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It says that every individual, regardless of age, has value, purpose and potential.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: It is about building workplace fairness through practical, step-by-step progress.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Kebun Baru)
text: Together, we can build a future, where seniors are not just included but celebrated, where experience is not just respected, but cherished.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As highlighted by the Minister for Manpower in his introductory comments, the Bill will provide protections against discrimination for employees who possess protected characteristics, while supporting the business needs of employers and our national objectives, including processes to preserve harmonious workplaces and resolve disputes amicably, as well as a range of levers to augment MOM’s education-first approach to address errant workplace practices.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Workplace fairness provides all Singaporeans the same opportunities to participate and contribute.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It ensures that the places we work are representative of the broader community and is a powerful contributor to an inclusive, cohesive and diverse society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Workplace fairness also assists to maximise the economic potential and competitive edge of employers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By broadening the diversity of its people, employers broaden the diversity of available talent, ideas and solutions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We would just naturally treat everyone the same.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is, however, a universal phenomenon that most humans treat certain types of people differently to others and Singapore is not immune to this peculiarity.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We all have our personal biases, preferences and prejudices; and it is not uncommon for these to consciously or unconsciously influence our thoughts and actions, including in the workplace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While my following comments focus heavily on women, I recognise that discrimination and disadvantage affects several other groups in our community, including people living with disabilities or mental illness; individuals from diverse racial, cultural and religious backgrounds; those from varying socio-economic and educational backgrounds; children and young people; older people; those with a criminal history; and people with carer responsibilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: As we move forward, we need to ensure that we recognise and address the individual needs and circumstances of all Singaporeans.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: They often face what I call the "triple squeeze" – managing career advancement, family responsibilities and societal expectations, all while navigating workplace biases that can be subtle yet significant.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The burden of proof for discrimination cases often rests on employees, making it difficult to address injustices effectively.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The so-called "motherhood penalty" significantly impacts career progression, with mothers perceived as less competent and thus less likely to be hired or promoted.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: They also face biased evaluations and are often given less challenging work upon returning from maternity leave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Ageism further marginalises older women, pushing them into manual labour roles despite their skills and penalising them for necessary health-related leave.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: And "career returners" face stereotypes of being less productive and adaptable, with insufficient support for reintegration into the workforce.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: To combat these issues, this Bill must address structural barriers related to gender stereotypes, particularly for minority women.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, it should include protections for foster parents as caregivers as well.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Furthermore, Mr Deputy Speaker, we must address the unique challenges faced by women returning to work after caregiving breaks.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While the Bill provides protection against discrimination, we also need practical measures to support the re-integration of women into the workplace, including, for example, structured return-to-work programmes, skills updating initiatives, mentorship schemes and flexible working arrangements during the transition period.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Even more troubling is the persistence of toxic workplace cultures.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Toxic workplace is a metaphor used to describe a place of work that is marked by significant personal conflicts between those who work there, including management.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: According to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, a toxic work environment is characterised by disrespectful, non-inclusive, unethical, cut-throat and abusive behaviours and attitudes.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: When capable professionals step back from leadership roles, underperform, or exit the workforce entirely due to their workplace culture, we all lose.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Combatting toxic workplace culture is not easy, but can be achieved and I would like to suggest some potential ways forward.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For example, regular respect, equity and diversity training for all staff, including senior managers and executives, the establishment of trained Respect, Equity and Diversity Officers in workplaces, in-house systems that routinely and anonymously seek the feedback of employees, enhanced in-house whistle-blowing mechanisms and protections and linking individual managerial reward and bonuses to independent assessments of workplace culture.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: While the reasons behind this decline are unclear, international data suggests that reasons may include: fear that speaking up will jeopardise their career, lack of knowledge about reporting mechanisms and lack of faith in the investigation process.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: The Ministry should also require all employers who prepare annual reports, to include in their annual report data on workplace diversity and inclusion trends and goals; number and outcome of discrimination complaints received and investigated; key strategies to address toxic workplace culture and create a harmonious and inclusive workplace environment.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill correctly prohibits discrimination based on "protected characteristics", such as nationality, age, gender and caregiving responsibilities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: However, I encourage the Ministry to either now, or in the future, extend the definition of protected characteristics to include, for example, criminal history.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen successful approaches in other jurisdictions that we might consider.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: For example, the UK's blind recruitment processes and structured interview protocols have shown promising results in reducing hiring bias.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Incorporating AI into these processes could be also useful.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: AI can help generate unbiased interviews and provide consistent evaluation metrics, reducing unconscious biasness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: By leveraging on AI, we can enhance the fairness and transparency of reporting and investigating procedures, ultimately contributing to a more equitable workplace.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: Other strategies could include recruiting, requiring recruitment panels to include members from varied backgrounds to minimise bias and promote diverse perspectives during the recruitment process, the development of mentorship programmes that pair employees from different backgrounds and in-house information and support networks for under-represented employees group, the use of data analytics to identify patterns of discrimination or bias within the organisation and to inform policy procedure and practice review.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is essential that we do not simply pass this Bill and assume that work is done.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: In closing, Mr Deputy Speaker, this Bill represents more than just legislation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It is a statement about the kind of society we want to be.

speaker: Assoc Prof Razwana Begum Abdul Rahim (Nominated Member)
text: It reflects that Singapore gives priority to fairness, respect, diversity and inclusion, and that workplace fairness is not just a legal requirement but a lived reality for all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Workplace Fairness Bill aims to foster fairer and more harmonious workplaces by protecting employees from unfair employment decisions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This Bill is the culmination of three years of efforts by the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Members have spoken on groups that will benefit from protection on the basis of age, nationality, sex, marital status, pregnancy, caregiving responsibilities, race, religion, language ability, disability and mental health condition.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Workplace Fairness Bill is an inclusive and progressive one, but it has a glaring carve-out.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are the only two characteristics that are expressly excluded from the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are we telling LGBTQ+ people that they are not protected from workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Are we telling employers that it is okay to discriminate against someone because of their sexual orientation and gender identity?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When we repealed section 377A, Minister Shanmugam explained, "The time has come for us to remove section 377A.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They do not deserve to be stigmatised because of their sexual orientation." By repealing 377A, Minister Shanmugam said that we will "start to deal with these divides, heal these divides, remove their pain".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But now, do we not think that we may deepen the stigmatisation by having our workplace fairness law single out sexual orientation and gender identity for exclusion?
