speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With this Bill, will we deepen the divides that we started to heal with the repeal of 377A?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill's carve-out of sexual orientation and gender identity is not merely hurtful to LGBTQ+ employees; it could also cause them to face additional workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Studies have shown that LGBTQ employees already face significant workplace discrimination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: One respondent to the NUS School of Public Health study, who is lesbian, said that a headhunter warned her against bringing up her sexual orientation at a job interview because a previous candidate had been rejected for mentioning their same-sex spouse.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another respondent, who is gay, said he was told by his employer that he would not be appointed to a managerial position because of his sexual orientation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, hiring managers and HR representatives themselves have described this same type of discrimination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Singapore LGBTQ+ Workforce Audit 2022, which polled 200 HR professionals and business leaders, found that only 64% of respondents said yes when asked if companies were open to recruiting and hiring diverse candidates, including LGBTQ individuals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is likely that the data understates the scale of the problem and that LGTBQ individuals are under-reporting the discrimination they face.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: From 2018 to 2022 none of the 312 workplace discrimination complaints received by TAFEP and MOM were related to discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The express exclusion of sexual orientation and gender identity from this law is likely to worsen this discrimination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Employers may think they are free to discriminate against LGBTQ employees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Employees may have the belief that TAFEP, TADM and MOM will not assist them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide a clear statement that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity in the workplace is wrong and unacceptable?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister also confirm that discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited under the TGFEP and Prevention from Harassment Act?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the Minister confirm that TAFEP, TADM, ECT and MOM will assist individuals who report being discriminated against at their workplace due to sexual orientation or gender identity and that LGBTQ+ individuals who face discrimination should feel safe to report workplace discrimination to TAFEP, TADM and MOM?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Moving forward, can the Minister share a timeline for reviewing protections against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The UK's Equality Act already includes sexual orientation as a protected characteristic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is the law that the Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness has cited as having had a positive impact on workplaces.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know that in Minister Tan's reply in Parliament in July 2023, he said that the Committee's recommendations were scoped tightly and to address the more common and familiar forms of discrimination.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: He said that it is better to take a measured first step, let stakeholders adjust to the new rules, before reviewing if more needs to be done.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I agree that our workplace fairness laws should be measured.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I welcome the suggestion that our laws will be reviewed and updated.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, it is one thing for the Bill to be silent on sexual orientation and gender identity and a very different thing for the Bill to expressly exclude sexual orientation and gender identity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, do we not feel this is a step back by reinforcing discrimination and promoting stigma against LGBTQ+ individuals?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In particular, I thank groups that have been speaking up against workplace discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They include Pink Dot SG, Oogachaga, Same But Different, SAFE, Project X, Q Chamber of Commerce, Action for Aids and AWARE.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are many, many more groups and individuals who have fought hard for a more inclusive Singapore, including for LGBTQ+ individuals.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While there are too many to name, I thank them too for their perseverance and advocacy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As former US President, Bill Clinton, said, "All of the country loses when any person is denied or forced out of a job because of sexual orientation.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: By way of explanation, outsourced workers are workers whose nature of work requires that they work on a permanent basis at a different location from their employer's premises.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These workers include cleaners, landscape workers and security officers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Outsourced workers' actual workplaces are therefore the external site that they are deployed at and the terms of deployment are subject to agreement between their employer and the service buyer, for example a Management Corporation Strata Title (MCST).

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: These workers often take instructions and are subject, to a large extent, to the management and instruction of service buyers or their managing agents.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I can cite examples I have seen myself.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: In a contract for the deployment of cleaners between an MCST and a cleaning company, a particular MCST had prescribed that the cleaners be of a particular race.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: I have also seen many security service tenders and contracts between MCSTs and security agencies that stipulate that officers must be younger than a particular age.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: The Security Association Singapore has publicly called out several MCSTs and managing agents over the past few years who have imposed discriminatory requirements and affected the workplace fairness of workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Such contractual requirements then trickle down to the employment practices of service providers, which become inherently discriminatory in order to meet their commercial contract obligations.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: While this may open the service provider, who is the employer by law, to penalties under the Act, the service buyers get away scot-free and can continue to stipulate discriminatory deployment practices pursuant to the service contract with the service provider.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: Many service buyers also impose liquidated damages on service providers if they do not comply with the discriminatory deployment requirements.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It is also not uncommon for service buyers to exercise, often in arbitrary fashion, the ability to axe the deployment of these workers at their site, often with immediate effect.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This affects workers' security of employment and peace of mind.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: It also creates an environment in which outsourced workers work perpetually in terrorem of the service buyer or managing agent at the site they are deployed to.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: There is therefore a significant lacuna in workplace protections that affects hundreds of thousands of outsourced workers.

speaker: Mr Raj Joshua Thomas (Nominated Member)
text: This will enable us to increase protections for our outsourced workers, and I hope that the respective tripartite partners can look into this urgently.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: The Minister for Manpower, Dr Tan See Leng.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We all recognise that this is a landmark Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are all balancing many considerations, across multiple stakeholders.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Some want to move quickly, move much further, but others, a lot more apprehensive, with significant trepidations and therefore, want to hold back.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will not be able to resolve all issues overnight.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But rest assured, we will continue to work on it and with all of your support, with all of your feedback, with all of your suggestions, we take them on board, we will work on it and we will improve over time.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What we all agree on, collectively today and this is really the type of unity we need to see across the entire House, is the need to create fairer workplaces which provide good opportunities for all of our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We are very, very thankful to have each and every one of you, those of you who have spoken and I am sure many more who have not found the opportunity to speak, within this House and beyond, on this journey, to build fairer workplaces for all of us.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And like I said, I want to reassure Members that we are listening closely.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Where there are suggestions that we are unable to take on board at this point in time, we will consider if they are suitable at a later stage as part of our regular review.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Just because we cannot agree at this point in time does not mean that it is a "no".

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We need to consider the entire ramifications with all the different permutations before we come to a nuanced solution.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Pritam Singh and Ms He Ting Ru said that the Government had disagreed with calls for an anti-discrimination law earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim – I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate her on behalf of all of us here in the House.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Perhaps, maybe you could join me in a round of applause.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: If it becomes untenable for businesses to operate in Singapore, this will affect jobs for Singaporeans and for our workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: What we do not want, is for the law to change the nature, to alter to such an extent the employer-employee relations, such that our workplaces become more litigious and more divided.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: But what we do want is for our workplaces, not just to remain, but to improve in terms of its fairness and harmonious nature.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Through our engagements, we know that employers generally do the right thing and they support fairer workplaces that contribute to better business outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We have tried to set the baseline standard with this Bill, recognising that employers need time to adjust to new requirements.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Jobseekers and employees also need time to understand how to use the new protections responsibly.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Even so, we have always been committed to this agenda, in response to the active advocacy from our Labour Members of Parliament.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We revisited this issue, the moment the COVID-19 pandemic abated.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We consulted widely, we deliberated extensively to put together a balanced Bill that preserves our current workplace norms and guards against divisions in our workplaces and society.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This includes the remaining 5% of complaints received.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This approach allows us to continue building our expertise in managing cases under the law, while ensuring that other characteristics remain protected from workplace discrimination under the guidelines.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In our surveys of many foreign jurisdictions, there are some areas that are heavily litigated.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It has also resulted in workers waiting years to have their case heard out in court and we know that justice delayed is justice denied.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Please let me reiterate: this does not mean that the other characteristics are any less important.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I just intend to address the questions that our Members have raised for the purpose of this debate.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Members like Mr Heng Chee How, Mr Sharael Taha and Mr Yip Hon Weng agreed with the need to address age discrimination and how we need to go beyond the Bill to fundamentally address perceptions and mindsets towards senior workers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This requires a multi-faceted approach, including adopting age-friendly workplace practices and addressing ingrained perceptions of ageism.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We agree and we will continue efforts to change mindsets on the ground.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our guidelines and resources will support training and job redesign to nurture more age-friendly workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Moving on to mental health issues, we agree with Mr Melvin Yong, Mr Keith Chua and Mr Yip Hon Weng's comments that beyond legislation, there is a need for greater education to stamp out stigma against those with mental health conditions and create more inclusive workplaces.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will continue to normalise conversations on mental health, share best practices with employers and co-workers to better support persons with mental health conditions and encourage help-seeking by individuals in distress.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Several Members – Miss Rachel Ong, Ms Denise Phua, Mr Ong Hua Han, Mr Chong Kee Hiong, Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr Sharael Taha, Ms He Ting Ru, Ms Jean See and Mr Saktiandi Supaat – raised the issue of reasonable accommodations for PwDs, including legislating it in the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We recognise the importance of reasonable accommodations in enabling PwDs to access and perform their jobs.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The Tripartite Committee on Workplace Fairness had observed that in other countries, the provision of reasonable accommodations was heavily litigated.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is a point that Mr Sharael Taha also acknowledged.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In Singapore, we have been able to improve employment outcomes for PwDs over the years through various measures, including under the Enabling Masterplan.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Hence, rather than at the outset, mandating employers to provide reasonable accommodations, we have embarked on an education first approach via the upcoming Tripartite Advisory.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We want to be able to shift and ultimately change mindsets and to mainstream the concept of reasonable accommodations in the employment space first, guiding employers and employees to discuss accommodations that will suit their specific work context.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: We will also work with the relevant partners, such as SG Enable and the trade associations and chambers to strengthen outreach to employers.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: And we want to reassure Members that these efforts will be taken concurrently with our preparations to implement the legislation.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Ong Hua Han, Ms Denise Phua and Ms He Ting Ru made various suggestions, including asking the Government to have a clear roadmap to mandate reasonable accommodations.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: My humble request to you is, let us focus, let us work hard on the education first approach, strengthen the understanding and support first, get the buy-in.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai suggested giving Singapore Citizens the first right to jobs over foreigners.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I believe that Singaporeans know that we need a calibrated position that will work well for our economy and our people, instead of swinging to the extremes.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Foreigners complement local workers to grow the economy and create job opportunities for Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Our workforce is small and in order to attract the best global companies here, we must allow them to also hire talent globally.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: At the same time, we recognise that our fellow Singaporeans are concerned about fair treatment and fair competition at the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: COMPASS encourages employers to develop their own local pipeline.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: It encourages employers to develop their own local pipeline and reduce their reliance on foreign talent, both generally and from a single source.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: The minimum cost of hiring EP and S Pass holders are also benchmarked to the top one-third of local PMETs and the Associate Professional and Technicians' wages respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This is to ensure a level playing field for locals.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: More fundamentally, we continue to invest in Singaporeans through lifelong upskilling, reskilling and career health initiatives, so that our fellow citizens are always well-placed to seize, to create better opportunities and build a better future for ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: This Bill adds to the suite of measures already in existence by further strengthening our ability to deter and to penalise discriminatory hiring practices.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Over the past decade, unemployment rate for Singapore Citizens has remained low at 3.2% on average.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Unlike what Mr Leong Mun Wai had tried to portray, there is no indication that underemployment is increasing.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: PMETs now make up 64% of all employed residents – up from 54% 10 years ago – matching the proportion of residents with tertiary education in the workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: In fact, the number of resident PMETs has grown faster than EP and S Pass holders between 2014 and 2024, the past decade.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Resident PMETs grew by 34% over this period, significantly higher than the EP and S Pass holders' increase of 11%.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Let us move on to other forms of discrimination not covered by the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: I want to start off by broadly addressing the concern of Members that the Bill does not cover all types of discrimination.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Again, let me re-emphasise that this Bill is just the start.

speaker: The Minister for Manpower (Dr Tan See Leng)
text: Like the song by the Carpenters: we have only just begun.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And we do so because we see the repeal of 377A and discrimination against LGBTQ individuals at the workplace as two very different issues, two separate issues.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I hope the call made by my colleague, Ms He Ting Ru, can be considered in future iterations, as the Minister shared that the Bill will be reviewed and it is akin to a work-in-progress and that this is just – not the first chapter – it is just the start.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: My point about raising the differences during the time of the repeal of the 377A was not to highlight differences, but to demonstrate that it is a complex issue.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And you can be rest assured that we are actively, actively sending our officers to overseas jurisdictions to get training, to see how they deal with it.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have also opened up access channels between the different groups, with TAFEP, with MOM, so that we, in the same way as we have built up experience, we have built up expertise in handling the 11 protected characteristics, we hope to be able to come to speed to also manage other characteristics.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In time to come, if we are able to reach a level where we are comfortable with and also, in terms of societal norms, it is always, like I have said in my concluding remarks, that we are always a work-in-progress and we will always want to improve our system.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would also help address the issue of under-reporting.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many might go on the website and realise it is not there, so they do not report it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, explicitly stating it might help with the under-reporting.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second point is on whether it is fair to just leave SOGI under the Tripartite Guidelines because of the penalties.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: So, if you discriminate against someone who is lesbian or gay and the penalty is you cannot hire foreigners, how would that make sense?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our sense is that, if you list it on a website, it may actually have a counter-effect that each and every single attribute has to be listed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If you do not list it, it means that it is not covered.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: By the way we have approached it, we have given enough reassurance.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the Member's point about whether the penalties, because of the fact that it is under TAFEP and TGFEP, whether it is sufficient, thus far, our experience is that when TAFEP calls up the company, they rarely, rarely dare to not comply.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If the hon Member, Mr Louis Ng, knows of any company after being called up by TAFEP, still ignores TAFEP's guidance, I would be very interested to know the company.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am not giving a name of the company now, but I thought again that the problem now is we do list certain characteristics on the TAFEP website.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We already state age, race, gender, religion, marital status, family, responsibility or disability.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: So, it is not a case where we do not state anything.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We do state some characteristic that is protected under TAFEP, but we just leave out again sexual orientation and gender identity, and that is the issue where the LGBTQ+ community feel that then, it is not fair.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: And we started off with these 11 protected characteristics because when we have enough experience, we have also got a treasure trove of information as to how to deal with them, let us grow.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Let us move ahead and as we accumulate more information, we can widen the reach.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I ask for the Members' understanding and support in that.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, this is surefooted, it is a prudent approach and it is also in tandem with our societal norms today and how we can move forward.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Minister's assurances will all be recorded in the Hansard.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: First, it is on three clauses: clause 12, clause 18 and clause 28.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: I asked about the age range for an infant.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Clarity is important because if the maximum age for who is deemed to be an infant is too low, a female worker may lose her protection when breastfeeding an older child.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: Hopefully, some clarity on this as we implement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: As currently worded, employers may get around clause 18 by not putting things in writing.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: And, finally, clause 28, I did ask a question earlier, hoping to get an answer.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (Pioneer)
text: So, in those other cases, would evidence of discrimination by the employer be relevant?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: On the definition, we certainly can take the Member's points and, like I said, we are still reviewing in terms of in the final Bill when it comes out.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Without appearing to be over-delegating, TAFEP will work on the other two items.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: From the perspective of even the definition of the age of an infant, should there be reasonable indication beyond even whatever the defined age is, because of extenuating circumstances, it is something that any sort of employee can bring up.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But, of course, the first thing that we hope to be able to get everyone into the same cadence is, first and foremost, because most employers are reasonable, the employee should try to resolve it through the grievance handling mechanism within the company.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If that does not work, come to us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We will, then, try to organise mediation and we believe that just the first two steps would resolve the vast majority of the cases.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that gives the Member that reassurance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Speaker, I have debated in this Parliament many times on the manpower policies and I have two questions to ask the Manpower Minister today.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am very concerned, having debated this Government over the last few years, that the Government seems to be very complacent about the effect of its foreign manpower policies on Singaporean workers – and every time the Manpower Minister has countered me with selected macro indicators.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Today, in the same fashion, I have said that low unemployment does not mean there is no significant under-employment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second question I want to ask is – this is also something that I have debated with the Manpower Minister over the years – just now, he had written off my assertion that low unemployment does not mean no significant under-employment.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: We know that this ratio is very corrupted, with original Singaporeans at the beginning of a period, new citizens that came in and new PRs.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, there is a lot of immigration effect on these macro indicators.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, did MOM look into a kind of pure indicator, rather than having all these effects and then, now, telling Singaporeans that the ratio has gone up from 50% to 60%?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But I do not see how they are related to the WFL.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that after this, we can come back to issues that are pertinent because we just had a seven-hour debate, starting from yesterday till now and we will continue.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Through my last four years, I am privileged and very honoured to be given the opportunity to be able to come to the highest office here, to be able to have this debate.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But Mr Leong Mun Wai has consistently been looking for a smoking gun.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The fact of the matter is that each time the Member asks for certain statistics, I give him the statistics.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: He would say that this is not what he is looking for.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Has he ever considered the fact that maybe something that he is looking for does not exist?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because of the fact that, after a while, the Member's cadence, my understanding has not changed.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Hence, I also pre-emptively prepared the statistics for him because I expected that he will bring it up today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Just to put it into perspective and I hope that, after this, Mr Speaker, Sir, may I humbly request that we just stick to the debate on the WFL?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I just wanted to tell the Member about foreign firms first.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If we talk about what kinds of jobs they offer, because they do hire a very high number of foreigners as well, but let me just give the Member the breakdown.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Foreign-owned firms provide high-paying jobs to our locals.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The median salaries of our resident employees working in foreign-owned firms are more than 70% higher compared to locals working in local-owned firms.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The Member talked about foreign high-skilled workforce displacing resident PMETs.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Resident PMETs grew by 34% over this period, significantly higher than the EP and S Pass holders' increase of 11%.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: As a result, the ratio of EP or S Pass to resident PMETs has improved, from one EP or S Pass holder for every three local PMETs in 2014 to now, one EP/S Pass holder for every four local PMET in 2024.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: This improvement is observed across most sectors, including the growth sectors of Information and Communications, Professional Services and Financial Services.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Has the labour market performance of locals been impacted by foreign workers?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Our locals continue to enjoy favourable employment outcomes.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Singapore leads globally in labour force participation rate of its residents and we are ahead of other major cities, such as Tokyo, Helsinki, Berlin and Hong Kong.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the last decade, incomes have grown across all percentiles, with the larger increases for lower income groups.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In the last five years, Singapore's real income growth is also higher than countries, such as the UK, US, Japan and Germany, many of whom are seeing income stagnation or declines.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I urge Mr Leong – we are here to pass this very landmark, historic Bill.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Some things we can try, but our total fertility rate continues to drop.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: The tax burden will start to shift to our future young.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, we are in this state of hyper competition all over the world.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Countries are competing, top companies are competing for global talent.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that we can work together, Mr Leong, for your grandchildren and my grandchildren.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: First of all, I would like to thank the Minister and his team in MOM for setting this landmark Bill forward.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: The first question is in terms of timeline, when will this Bill be implemented?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am not sure whether I missed the exact date in his speech.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But can the Minister share when the implementation would be?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am aware that there is going to be another Bill with regard to the ECT.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Second is, in terms of, I heard the word TAFEP mentioned many times in this Bill and me being in the TAFEP Committee – and I have seen the TAFEP staff and resource constraints there and how much good work they have done.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: Can the Minister share, in terms of budget and in terms of resources, going forward, after the implementation, whether there will be more resources for TAFEP?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We have not passed the Bill today, yet.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: We are tightening TGFEP, because we need to ensure that it continues to support WFL well.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: At the same time, we have also committed to reasonable accommodations, how we want to step up education efforts, grievance handling and so on and so forth.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, there is a lot of work to be done and all that will move simultaneously so that by the time the Bill is up and fully implemented, all of the other supporting entities will be ready.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I know that embedded in the Member's second question is that we will, indeed, be reviewing and, hopefully, increasing the resources of TAFEP.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I will personally appeal to the Prime Minister and the Minister for Finance for that.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I missed out another clarification for the Minister pertaining to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I have asked some questions on clause 31.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What is the range of the penalties that the Bill envisages, vis-a-vis, clause 31(A) to (I)?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: The second clarification, pertaining to clause 31, again, is whether the Ministry intends for the companies that commit violations and are subject to administrative penalties, whether they will be named and if not named, at least the circumstances of their infractions made public so workers and employees alike would be educated.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I have to admit, I am not a lawyer.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: With regard to naming, what we intend to do is that for the breaches, our first approach is to engage them and provide an education first approach.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Because our basic intention is that, thus far, it has worked well for us.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not think that a particular employer would have intended or set it up to discriminate, unless they are very egregious.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: In which case, then, there will be the administrative and, on top of that, there will be the civil penalties.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But what we intend to do is engage them, educate them, point them to the right resources, the help and to see how we can also help them and educate them.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But, thus far, from our past experiences, each time when TAFEP engages the companies, they have been very, very understanding and they have been very compliant.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I hope that gives the Member that reassurance.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: I just have one very brief question for the Minister.

speaker: Ms Usha Chandradas
text: Does the Ministry have a window of time in mind, after which it will review the definition of the protected characteristic of sex, as it is set out in clauses 8C and 10?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: For the time itself, we need to cross the bridge first and, after crossing the bridge, work out the rest of the subsidiary legislations.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: Post-implementation, we can have greater clarity before we can commit to a particular timeline.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: But the reassurance that I want to share with Ms Usha is that we will constantly review.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am sure that given the universal huge amount of interest in this particular Bill, I am sure we will be kept on our toes.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I would just like to confirm that the MOM has not done any study into under-employment?

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I do not intend to interrupt, but I have already made it clear.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: So, can we please focus on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ideally, if you have clarifications, ask them all at one go, do not to break it up.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, the Minister also denied that the effect of immigration has not altered his conclusion on the PME ratio that he had raised?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because the PME ratio is not a pure ratio.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: You mentioned that you had a clarification to his response.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Can he clarify that MOM has confirmed that the effect of immigration has not altered the conclusion of the PME ratio that he has raised?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Because he is trying to say that there is no under-employment, Singaporean PMEs are doing well.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: It is because there is low unemployment, it is because the PME ratio is increasing.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: So, I raised my point because every economic indicator the Minister has raised, I can actually raise a lot of issues about it, as I am an economics statistician.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Mr Leong, then I suggest, maybe, if you have specific points to ask, you could file a PQ on them, with the specifics and ask your questions.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But we can get an answer from the Minister now.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I am sorry, Mr Speaker, I thought you told me to sit down.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: I did not respond because I do not see how it is relevant to our debate on WFL today.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: If Mr Leong Mun Wai has a separate PQ, as how Mr Speaker has also appropriately advised, he can file a PQ.

speaker: Dr Tan See Leng
text: MOM will never step away from answering his PQ.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: We have spent a long time discussing this.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: The Minister has also given a very comprehensive reply.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will now put the question to the House.      .

speaker: The Chairman
text: The citation year "2024" will be changed to "2025" as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.
